index.html.summary: MGM Character Controller MGM Character Controller is a modular, high-performance character locomotion package for Unity 6, built entirely on the DOTS stack (Entities, Unity.Physics, Burst, Jobs). It provides a state-machine-driven approach to character movement with full source generation, making it both easy to extend and blazingly fast at runtime. When to Use This Package Use MGM Character Controller when you need: A kinematic character controller built on Unity ECS State-machine-driven movement with clear per-state lifecycle hooks Burst-compiled parallel locomotion for many characters Clean separation between physics simulation (ECS) and presentation (GameObjects) This package is not for projects that use MonoBehaviour-based character controllers, do not use Unity DOTS, or need a drop-in replacement for Unity's built-in CharacterController component. Key Features Pure ECS locomotion with Burst-compiled jobs for maximum throughput State-machine-driven movement with a clear lifecycle per state Source-generated boilerplate via Roslyn analyzers, so you focus on gameplay logic Collide-and-slide physics with automatic step detection, slope handling, and ground snapping Moving platform support with velocity inheritance and rotation handling Hybrid GameObject layer for seamless integration with animations, audio, and cameras Built-in debug visualization for contact points, movement paths, and collision impulses Editor scaffolding tools that generate the entire state machine folder structure in one click Limitations Characters are kinematic only - no ragdoll or force-driven movement out of the box Profile changes require re-baking (exit and re-enter Play mode) Debug visualization is editor-only and adds overhead when enabled No built-in animation state machine bridge (you connect your Animator on the model GameObject) Quick Links Installation - Install the package and verify it works Quickstart - Import the sample and see a character running in minutes Getting Started - Create your first character from scratch Architecture Overview - How the pieces fit together The Execution Loop - What happens each fixed update Creating a State Machine - Step-by-step guide Writing Custom States - The state lifecycle in depth Samples - Sample index with study order Troubleshooting - Common issues and fixes API Reference - Full API documentation Requirements Requirement Version Unity 6000.3+ Entities 1.3.9 Unity.Physics 1.3.8 Burst 1.8.18 Collections 2.5.4 Mathematics 1.3.2 Package Info Package name wayn.games.mgm.character-controller Version 0.8.0 Author WAYN Games License See LICENSE.md Next Step If you already have the package installed, go to the Quickstart. Otherwise, start with Installation.

manual/architecture.html.title: Architecture Overview | MGM Character Controller
manual/architecture.html.summary:
Architecture Overview This page explains the high-level design of the MGM Character Controller: the entity types, the role of each layer, and how data flows through the system. Design Philosophy The package is built around three principles: Performance first - All locomotion logic runs in Burst-compiled parallel jobs. No managed allocations on the hot path. Separation of concerns - Physics simulation (ECS) is decoupled from presentation (GameObjects). You can run thousands of characters without any GameObjects at all. Extensibility through composition - Instead of a monolithic character controller, you compose behavior from a state machine, a physics profile, an input component, and a context, all of which are user-defined types. Entity Types The package defines three distinct entity roles. Understanding them is essential. Locomotor (Pure ECS) The Locomotor is the primary character entity. It lives entirely in ECS and carries all the components needed for physics-based movement: Component Purpose LocalTransform World position and rotation PhysicsCollider Capsule collider for collision detection PhysicsVelocity Required by Unity.Physics to consider the character a non static entity. (always zeroed; the package drives movement directly) LocomotionVelocity The character's actual velocity, maintained by the state machine LocomotionGravity Gravity vector applied to this character LocomotionContact Current surface contact information (normal, type, entity) CharacterPhysicsProfileBlob Baked physics configuration (capsule size, mass, slopes) LocomotionProfileBlob Baked gameplay profile (speeds, jump force, etc.) TStateMachine Source-generated state machine component (current state + dispatch) TInput User-defined input component TStateData User-defined per-state persistent data The Locomotor is a kinematic body. Unlike Unity.Physics dynamic bodies, it does not respond to forces automatically. Instead, the locomotion job computes displacement each frame and moves the collider through the world using a collide-and-slide algorithm. Model (Hybrid ECS + GameObject) The Model is an optional entity that provides visual representation. It carries a reference to a GameObject prefab that gets instantiated at runtime. The model entity follows the Locomotor entity via the CharacterFollower component. Why separate them? Because: Locomotion logic runs in parallel Burst jobs that cannot touch GameObjects Visual updates (animation, particles, audio) need MonoBehaviour access You can run headless simulations (server, AI training) with zero GameObjects Player (Input Source) The Player entity represents an input source. It owns a ControlledCharacters buffer that lists which Locomotor entities it controls. A Player also has: A PlayerGameObjectPrefab referencing a GameObject with camera, input system, and UI A PlayerGameObjectInstance linking to the instantiated runtime copy An LocomotionInputAsset that reads hardware input and maps it to the input component Players are managed by the PlayerGoManagerSystem, which instantiates and destroys their GameObjects as players join and leave. Assembly Structure The package is split into three runtime assemblies: WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Runtime Core ECS logic (state machine, physics, components, systems) WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Hybrid GameObject bridge (transform sync, entity-GO mapping) WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Editor Editor tools (scaffolding, inspectors) Your game code references Runtime and optionally Hybrid. The Editor assembly is editor-only and provides scaffolding menus. Data Flow Here is how data flows through the system each fixed update: flowchart TD HW["Hardware Input"] PIA["PlayerInputAsset.ReadInputsFromAsset()
MonoBehaviour, Update rate"] ICI["ICharacterLocomotionInput.ApplyInputsToCharacter()
Accumulates triggers"] IRS["InputReaderSystem (generated)
Fixed update, writes TInput component"] LJ["LocomotionJob (Burst, parallel)
Fixed update, reads all components"] TR["Transform updated on Locomotor entity"] CFS["CharacterFollowerSystem
Syncs Model entity to Locomotor"] EGO["EntityGoTransformSyncSystem (Hybrid)
Copies entity transforms to GameObjects"] GO["GameObject renders on screen"] HW --> PIA --> ICI --> IRS --> LJ subgraph LocomotionJob S1["HandleExternalImpulses"] S2["Integrate"] S3["SolveOverlaps"] S4["CollideAndSlide (loop)"] S5["SnapToGround"] S6["InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity"] S7["EvaluateTransition"] S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 --> S5 --> S6 --> S7 end LJ --> LocomotionJob --> TR --> CFS --> EGO --> GO Source Generation A Roslyn source generator reads your anchor struct annotated with [LocomotionStateMachine] and your state structs annotated with [LocomotionState] and produces: State machine component - An IComponentData struct that holds the current state and dispatches to the correct state implementation Locomotion system - An ISystem that schedules the LocomotionJob each fixed update Input reader system - An ISystem that reads input from the PlayerInputAsset and writes it to the TInput component Player input manager - Manages per-player input asset instances This means you never write scheduling code, component type handle boilerplate, or state dispatch switch statements. You define your states, annotate your structs, and the generator handles the rest. Blob Assets Configuration data (physics profiles, locomotion profiles, debug config) is stored as blob assets rather than regular components. Blob assets are: Immutable at runtime (safe for parallel access) Shared across entities with identical configuration (memory efficient) Created during baking from ScriptableObject authoring assets This means changing a profile value requires re-baking (exiting and re-entering play mode, or modifying the asset in the editor). Next Steps The Execution Loop - Detailed breakdown of each step in the locomotion job Creating a State Machine - How to define your own state machine Samples - Study the sample code to see this architecture in practice

manual/best-practices.html.title: Best Practices | MGM Character Controller
manual/best-practices.html.summary: Best Practices Opinionated recommendations for building with the MGM Character Controller. Project Structure One state machine per character archetype Create separate state machine types for characters with fundamentally different movement (e.g., ground characters vs vehicles vs flying). Do not try to fit all movement into a single state enum. Keep states small and focused Each state should handle one movement behavior. If a state has many branches ("if grounded do X, else if swimming do Y, else..."), split it into separate states with transitions between them. Use sub-profiles for each state Group profile parameters by the state that uses them: public partial struct MyProfile : ILocomotionProfile { public MovingProfile Moving; public FallingProfile Falling; public JumpingProfile Jumping; public DashProfile Dash; } This keeps the Inspector organized and makes it obvious which parameters affect which state. State Logic Always use ref access for BaseContext Declare a ref local at the top of your state methods to avoid copy-modify-writeback overhead: public void OnIntegrateState(ref MyContext ctx) { ref BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ref ctx.BaseContext; // All modifications go through the ref } Exception: OnResolveStateCollisions requires copy-modify-writeback because Move() modifies the context internally. Accumulate triggers, overwrite continuous inputs In ApplyInputsToCharacter: Continuous (movement direction, aim): overwrite with the latest value Triggers (jump, dash, fire): accumulate with += Always consume triggers in your state logic by resetting them to zero after reading. Share computation logic, not state Use behavior structs to share physics computations across states - small stateless structs with configuration fields and an Integrate method returning an acceleration (e.g., the sample's GravityBehavior, shared by Falling and Sliding, or HorizontalLocomotionBehavior, shared by Moving and Jumping). The state constructs the behavior from its profile data, calls Integrate, and commits the result. Do not share state data - each state should manage its own initialization and cleanup via OnEnterState / OnExitState. Do not add platform velocity manually The ComputeInheritedDisplacement step handles platform velocity automatically. Adding it in OnIntegrateState causes double-application. The only exception is OnEnterState for airborne states (e.g., jumping off a platform), where you add PlatformHorizontalVelocity to the character's own velocity to preserve momentum. Transitions Use the [LocomotionTransition] attribute pattern Declare transitions as small structs with [LocomotionTransition] and control priority with [EvaluateBefore] / [EvaluateAfter]: [LocomotionTransition(typeof(IdleState), typeof(JumpingState))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(IdleToMoving))] public struct IdleToJumping : IMyTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref MyContext ctx) => ctx.BaseContext.IsGroundingContact && ctx.Input.JumpTrigger > 0; } This is the only supported pattern - the source generator discovers the structs, orders them, and handles dispatch and the exit/enter calls. Put critical transitions first Order transitions so the most important ones evaluate first. Typical priority: jump > move > fall > slide. A [EvaluateBefore] on jump over move ensures pressing jump while running works. Performance Keep all state code Burst-compatible Avoid managed types (strings, classes, arrays) in state logic - states run inside Burst-compiled jobs No managed types (string, class, arrays) in state, context, profile, input, or state data structs Use shared colliders By default, capsule colliders are shared across entities with identical geometry and filter settings. Only add ForceUniqueColliderAuthoring if you need runtime shape modification per entity. Use shared profile blob assets All entities referencing the same profile asset share the same blob memory. Design your profiles so that common character types use the same asset. Only enable debug visualization when investigating Debug components add dynamic buffers and per-frame recording overhead. Remove LocomotionDebugConfigAuthoring from entities you are not actively debugging. Debugging Use debug visualization before adding logs The built-in debug visualization shows contact points, movement paths, and impulses per execution stage. This is faster than logging and works inside Burst jobs. Check transition priority when states misbehave If a character enters the wrong state, check [EvaluateBefore] ordering. A higher-priority transition may be firing before the one you expect. Verify contact types Many issues come from incorrect contact classification. Log or inspect ctx.BaseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO.ContactType to confirm whether the surface is Ground, Wall, or Ceiling. Team Workflow One profile asset per character class Use ScriptableObject profile assets so designers can tune parameters without touching code. Check these assets into version control. Name states and transitions descriptively Use the {Source}To{Target} naming convention for transitions (e.g., IdleToJumping, FallingToMoving). This makes the transition graph readable at a glance. Test states in isolation When adding a new state, start with just one transition into it and one transition out. Verify the core behavior works before wiring up all transitions. Next Steps Writing Custom States - State lifecycle reference Extending the Package - Advanced customization Troubleshooting - Common issues and fixes

manual/creating-state-machine.html.title: Creating a State Machine | MGM Character Controller
manual/creating-state-machine.html.summary: Creating a State Machine This guide explains how to create a complete locomotion state machine from scratch, either using the editor scaffolding tool or by hand. Using the Editor Tool (Recommended) The fastest way to create a state machine is through the Unity editor menu: Right-click in the Project window where you want the state machine folder Select Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller > StateMachine Type a name for your state machine (e.g., Vehicle, Swimming, Flying) Press Enter The tool generates all required files with proper naming, namespaces, and wiring. You can immediately start customizing the generated code. Understanding What Gets Generated When you create a state machine named MyCharacter, the tool generates these types: The Anchor Struct [LocomotionStateMachine] public partial struct MyCharacterStateMachine { } This struct is the heart of the state machine. The [LocomotionStateMachine] attribute is parameterless - all type names are derived by convention from the struct name. For MyCharacterStateMachine, the prefix MyCharacter produces: MyCharacterContext, MyCharacterProfile, MyCharacterInput, MyCharacterStateData, and MyCharacterStates (the generated enum). States are separate structs annotated with [LocomotionState], linking them back to the state machine: [LocomotionState(typeof(MyCharacterStateMachine))] public partial struct IdleState { } The Context The context struct is source-generated from the anchor struct. You do not write it yourself. The generated struct looks like: // Source-generated - do not create manually public partial struct MyCharacterContext : ILocomotionContext<MyCharacterProfile, MyCharacterInput, MyCharacterStateData> { public BaseLocomotionContext BaseContext { get; set; } public CharacterPhysicsProfile CharacterPhysicsProfile { get; set; } public MyCharacterProfile Profile { get; set; } public MyCharacterInput Input { get; set; } public MyCharacterStateData StateData { get; set; } } The context is a data bag that is passed by reference through every state lifecycle method. It wraps: BaseLocomotionContext - The core physics state (position, velocity, displacement, contacts, gravity) CharacterPhysicsProfile - The baked capsule/physics configuration Your custom profile, input, and state data Because the context is partial, you can add custom properties and method overrides (like ComputeGroundSnappingDistance) in your own partial declaration. Tip If you frequently modify BaseContext fields, declare it as a public field in your partial declaration rather than using the auto-property. This lets you use ref access: ref BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ref ctx.BaseContext; The Profile [Serializable] public partial struct MyCharacterProfile { // Add your configuration fields here: // public float MaxSpeed; // public float JumpForce; } The ILocomotionProfile interface is added automatically by the source generator via the partial mechanism. Profile data is baked into a blob asset during entity conversion. It is immutable at runtime and shared across all entities that reference the same profile asset. Put all tunable gameplay parameters here. The Input public partial struct MyCharacterInput { // Add your input fields here: // public float3 Movement; // public float JumpTrigger; public void ApplyInputsToCharacter(in MyCharacterInput playerInputs) { // Copy or accumulate input values here } } The ICharacterLocomotionInput<MyCharacterInput> and IComponentData interfaces are added automatically by the source generator via the partial mechanism. The input struct is an ECS component. It receives values from the PlayerInputAsset at the Update rate and accumulates them for the fixed update. The ApplyInputsToCharacter method is called every Update frame by the generated input reader system. Warning Trigger inputs (like jump) must be accumulated, not overwritten. If the Update rate is higher than the fixed update rate, a trigger press could be missed. Accumulate with JumpTrigger += playerInputs.JumpTrigger and consume it in your state logic by resetting it to zero. The StateData public partial struct MyCharacterStateData { // Add per-state persistent data here: // public int JumpCount; // public float StateTimer; } The IComponentData interface is added automatically by the source generator via the partial mechanism. State data persists across frames and state transitions. Unlike the context (which is rebuilt each frame from components), state data is stored as an ECS component and survives between frames. The Profile Asset [CreateAssetMenu(...)] public class MyCharacterProfileAsset : LocomotionProfileAsset<MyCharacterProfile> { // Serialized fields matching your profile struct public override ref MyCharacterProfile BuildBlobAsset(ref BlobBuilder blobBuilder) { ref MyCharacterProfile profile = ref blobBuilder.ConstructRoot<MyCharacterProfile>(); // Copy serialized fields to blob return ref profile; } } This ScriptableObject is what you assign in the Inspector. It serializes your profile data and builds the blob asset during baking. The Input Asset [CreateAssetMenu(...)] public class MyCharacterPlayerInputAsset : PlayerInputAsset<MyCharacterInput> { public override void ReadInputsFromAsset(out MyCharacterInput inputs) { // Read from Input System and populate inputs } public override void InitInputAsset(PlayerGameObjectInstance instance) { // Cache camera, PlayerInput component, etc. } } The input asset reads hardware input and converts it to your input struct. It is a ScriptableObject that gets instantiated per player at runtime, so each player can cache their own camera and input device references. The Authoring Components Two authoring MonoBehaviours are generated: Character Locomotor Authoring - Placed on the character entity in the sub-scene. References the profile asset and configures the physics profile. Player Character Authoring - Placed on the player entity. References the character to control and the input asset. The Locomotion System The locomotion system is fully source-generated. It implements ILocomotionSystem<TStateMachine, TStates, TContext, TProfile, TInput, TStateData> and ISystem, scheduling the LocomotionJob each fixed update. You never need to write this system yourself. To customize system behavior, override the DIM lifecycle methods (OnLocomotionSystemCreate, OnLocomotionSystemUpdate, OnLocomotionSystemDestroy) via a partial interface declaration. See Customizing the Locomotion System for details. What the Source Generator Produces In addition to the files you write, the Roslyn source generator produces (at compile time, invisible in the Project window): State machine component (MyCharacterStateMachine) - An IComponentData struct with a CurrentState field and dispatch methods that call the correct state implementation based on the enum value Input reader system - Reads from the PlayerInputAsset each Update frame and writes to the TInput component ISystem lifecycle methods - Generated OnCreate, OnUpdate, and OnDestroy on your locomotion system struct that schedule the LocomotionJob and manage type handles You never need to write or maintain this code. The generator reads your enum and produces it automatically. Adding a New State After the initial generation, use the editor menu to add states: Right-click in the Project window Select Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller > State Name the state (e.g., Swimming) This generates a new state struct file annotated with [LocomotionState(typeof(MyCharacterStateMachine))]. The source generator automatically adds the state to the generated enum. Alternatively, create the state struct manually and annotate it with [LocomotionState(typeof(YourStateMachine))]. See Writing Custom States for the struct template. Manual Creation If you prefer to create everything by hand (or need to understand what the tools do), follow this checklist: Create an anchor partial struct with [LocomotionStateMachine] attribute (e.g., MyCharacterStateMachine) Create a partial struct for profile data (named {Prefix}Profile) Create a partial struct for input data with ApplyInputsToCharacter (named {Prefix}Input) Create a partial struct for state data (named {Prefix}StateData) Create at least one state partial struct with [LocomotionState(typeof(YourStateMachine))] Create a LocomotionProfileAsset<TProfile> ScriptableObject Create a PlayerInputAsset<TInput> ScriptableObject Register the generic input component: [assembly: RegisterGenericComponentType(typeof(LocomotionInputAsset<TInput>))] The source generator produces the context struct, state enum, locomotion system, authoring components, and all interface implementations from these inputs. The editor tool does all of this in one click, which is why it is recommended. Next Steps Writing Custom States - Implement state logic The Execution Loop - Understand when each method is called Recipe: Add a New Transition - Wire up transitions between states Samples - See a complete state machine implementation

manual/debug-visualization.html.title: Debug Visualization | MGM Character Controller
manual/debug-visualization.html.summary: Debug Visualization The MGM Character Controller includes a built-in debug visualization system that renders contact points, movement paths, and collision impulses directly in the Scene view. This is invaluable for diagnosing movement issues, tuning physics parameters, and understanding what the locomotion system is doing each frame. Enabling Debug Visualization Debug visualization is opt-in per entity: Select the character entity's authoring GameObject in the sub-scene Add a LocomotionDebugConfigAuthoring component Configure which visualizations you want to see Enter Play mode The debug config is baked into a blob asset, so changes require re-entering Play mode. Debug Data Types Path Points Path points show the character's position at each stage of the execution loop. They visualize the trajectory the character takes through a single frame, including each bounce of the collide-and-slide algorithm. Contact Points Contact points mark where the character's collider touches the environment. They are color-coded by contact type: Contact Type What It Means Ground The surface is walkable (slope below MaxSlope) Wall The surface is too steep to walk on Ceiling The surface is above the character None No contact this frame Impulse Points Impulse points show where collision forces are applied, both forces the character receives and forces it applies to other bodies. These help diagnose unexpected velocity changes or interactions with dynamic objects. Debug Stages Each visualization point is tagged with the execution stage where it was recorded: Stage Description Start Before any processing SolveOverlaps After overlap resolution CollideAndSlide After collide-and-slide SnapToGround After the ground snapping step InheritDisplacement After platform velocity computation This lets you pinpoint exactly which stage is producing unexpected behavior. Components and Systems LocomotionDebugConfig A blob asset storing debug configuration per entity. Controls visualization through duration floats (PathSeconds, ContactSeconds, ImpulseSeconds) - a duration of zero or less disables that category - and per-stage/per-type color and shape settings. LocomotionDebugRecorder A static utility that records debug points into dynamic buffers during job execution. Called from within the locomotion job when debug buffers are present. Debug Buffers Three IBufferElementData types store the recorded points: LocomotionDebugPathPoint - Position + stage + frame index LocomotionDebugContactPoint - Position + normal + contact type + body type + frame index LocomotionDebugImpulsePoint - Position + direction + magnitude + body type + is-applied flag + frame index LocomotionDebugDisplaySystem Reads the debug buffers and renders visualizations using the Unity.DebugDisplay API (Burst-compatible line and arrow drawing via PhysicsDebugDisplaySystem). LocomotionDebugFrameCounterSystem Maintains a global frame counter used to tag debug points. This allows the display system to distinguish between points from different frames and optionally show history. Performance Considerations Debug visualization adds overhead: Memory: Each entity with debug enabled allocates three dynamic buffers that grow each frame CPU: Recording points in the locomotion job adds branch checks and buffer writes Rendering: Drawing gizmos happens on the main thread For this reason: Only enable debug on entities you are actively investigating Disable debug visualization in builds The debug components are automatically excluded when the authoring component is not present Custom Debug Inspector The LocomotionDebugConfigAuthoringEditor provides a custom Inspector for the debug config authoring component. It shows a visual preview of the configured debug options including duration settings, colors, and contact shapes. Tips for Debugging Character falls through ground Enable path points and ground snap visualization. Check if: The snap-to-ground capsule cast is reaching the ground (path point should show a downward segment) The contact type at the end of the frame is Ground Character gets stuck on walls Enable contact points. Check if: The contact is classified as Wall vs Ground The MaxSlope threshold is correct Step detection is attempting and failing (check MaxStepHeight) Character launched unexpectedly Enable impulse points. Check if: External impulses are being applied (from CharacterContactSystem) A dynamic body collision is injecting unexpected velocity Platform inheritance is double-applied State transitions not firing This is a logic issue, not a physics issue. Add Debug.Log calls in your transition helper methods (temporarily, for non-Burst debugging) or check the state machine component in the Entity Inspector. Profiler Integration Beyond visual debugging, the package integrates with Unity's Profiler: ProfilerMarkerExtensions Burst-compiled profiler marker utilities that add custom markers to the Profiler timeline. These markers show up under the locomotion job's execution, helping you identify which stage is consuming the most time. Next Steps The Execution Loop - Understand what each debug stage corresponds to Physics Configuration - Tuning parameters informed by debug data Troubleshooting - Common issues and how debug visualization helps diagnose them

manual/execution-loop.html.title: The Execution Loop | MGM Character Controller
manual/execution-loop.html.summary:
The Execution Loop Every fixed update, the locomotion job processes each character entity through a precise sequence of steps. Understanding this sequence is critical for writing correct state logic. Overview The locomotion job runs as a Burst-compiled IJobChunk scheduled in the FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup, after the physics step. Each character is processed independently and in parallel. The tick rate itself is authorable — see Fixed Step Rate. The steps execute in this exact order: flowchart TD START(["Frame Start"]) subgraph S1["1. HandleExternalImpulses"] HEI["Accumulate velocity impulses
from CharacterContactSystem"] end subgraph S2["2. Integrate - OnIntegrateState"] INT["Compute velocities + displacement"] end subgraph S3["3. SolveOverlaps"] SO["Multi-plane de-collision
Sets OverlapState: None | Push | Pinch | Crush"] end subgraph S4["4. CollideAndSlide"] CAS_CRUSH{"OverlapState
== Crush?"} CAS_LOOP{"HasRemaining-
Displacement &&
bounce < MaxBounce?"} CAS["OnResolveStateCollisions
Project, cast, slide,
update contacts"] CAS_NEW{"New contact?"} CAS_OC["OnCollision"] CAS_CRUSH -- Yes --> CAS_END CAS_CRUSH -- No --> CAS_LOOP CAS_LOOP -- Yes --> CAS --> CAS_NEW CAS_NEW -- Yes --> CAS_OC --> CAS_LOOP CAS_NEW -- No --> CAS_LOOP CAS_LOOP -- No --> CAS_END CAS_END([done]) end subgraph S5["5. SnapToGround"] SNAP_NONE{"ContactType
== None?"} SNAP_UP{"Moving upward?

Snap position + update contact"] SNAP_NONE -- "Yes (skip)" --> SNAP_END SNAP_NONE -- No --> SNAP_UP SNAP_UP -- "Yes (clear contact)" --> SNAP_END SNAP_UP -- No --> SNAP_VVEL SNAP_VVEL -- "No (skip)" --> SNAP_END SNAP_VVEL -- "Yes (at rest)" --> SNAP --> SNAP_END SNAP_END([done]) end subgraph S6["6. InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity"] IH_GROUND{"Grounding
contact?"} IH_CRUSH{"Crush?"} IH_DYN{"Standing on
dynamic body?"} IH["Compute + apply platform displacement
Apply twist rotation"] IH_GROUND -- No --> IH_END IH_GROUND -- Yes --> IH_CRUSH IH_CRUSH -- Yes --> IH_END IH_CRUSH -- No --> IH_DYN IH_DYN -- No --> IH_END IH_DYN -- Yes --> IH --> IH_END IH_END([done]) end subgraph S7["7. EvaluateTransition"] ET["Source-generated dispatch
to LocomotionTransition structs"] end DONE(["Frame End"]) START --> HEI HEI --> INT INT --> SO SO --> CAS_CRUSH CAS_END --> SNAP_NONE SNAP_END --> IH_GROUND IH_END --> ET ET --> DONE Each step in the pipeline is a default interface method (DIM) on ILocomotionStateMachine that can be overridden on your state machine's partial struct. See Customizing the Execution Pipeline for details. There is no OnUpdateState method. The integration and collision resolution phases together form the "update" of your state. Transitions are evaluated once, at the very end, after all physics is resolved. The step ordering and semantics are pinned by the technical contract shipped with the package (Documentation~/spec/technical-contract.md), and the geometry of the cast capsule used by the pipeline's physics queries is specified as GEO-1 in the behavior specification (Documentation~/spec/). Step-by-Step Breakdown 1. HandleExternalImpulses The CharacterContactSystem runs during the PhysicsSimulationGroup (between contact creation and jacobian creation) and collects velocity impulses from external sources, such as: Dynamic rigid bodies that have collided with the character Other characters pushing against this one Explosions or force fields These impulses are applied to the character's velocity before your state logic runs, so your OnIntegrateState sees the updated velocity. This is why you should not clear velocity unconditionally at the start of integration unless you intend to discard external forces. 2. Integrate (OnIntegrateState) This is where your state logic computes velocities and displacements for the current frame. The system calls your state's OnIntegrateState method. In this step, you should: Compute acceleration from input (movement direction, jump force) Apply gravity acceleration Call baseContext.UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements() to convert velocities into displacements What you should NOT do here: Move the character's position directly (that happens in the collision step) Add platform velocity (the ComputeInheritedDisplacement step handles that automatically) Read contact information from this frame (contacts haven't been resolved yet; you see last frame's contacts) The Kinematic Equation UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements applies the standard kinematic equations: displacement += velocity * dt + 0.5f * acceleration * dt * dt; velocity += acceleration * dt; This is done separately for horizontal and vertical components, allowing different behavior for each (e.g., gravity only affects vertical, movement input only affects horizontal). 3. SolveOverlaps After integration, the system checks whether the character's collider is currently overlapping with any other collider. This can happen when: A moving platform pushes the character into a wall Another character occupies the same space The character was teleported into geometry The overlap solver attempts to push the character out of the overlap. If it cannot (e.g., the character is pinched between two moving surfaces), it tracks the overlap state: OverlapState Meaning None No overlap detected Push Character was pushed out successfully Pinch Character is squeezed but not fully trapped Crush Character is fully embedded with no escape You can read ctx.BaseContext.OverlapState in your state logic to react to crushing situations (e.g., kill the character). 4. CollideAndSlide (OnResolveStateCollisions + OnCollision) After integration computes the desired displacement, the character needs to actually move through the world while respecting colliders. This is the collide-and-slide loop. The system invokes your state's OnResolveStateCollisions as long as there is remaining displacement, up to CharacterPhysicsProfile.MaxBounce iterations. This multi-bounce approach allows the character to slide along walls, step over obstacles, and navigate complex geometry. After each iteration, if a new contact was detected (the contact changed during Move() and the result is not None), the system calls your state's OnCollision hook. This lets you react to specific surfaces (trampolines, damage zones) without replacing the default collision resolution. See Recipe: Customize Collision Response. Default Behavior If you do not override OnResolveStateCollisions, the default DIM calls baseContext.Move(), which performs two operations: Displacement correction - Adjusts HorizontalDisplacement and VerticalDisplacement based on the current contact type: Contact Type Behavior None Displacement is applied as-is (free movement in air) Ground Vertical displacement is cancelled; horizontal displacement follows the ground slope Wall Step detection is attempted; if not a step, displacement is projected along the wall surface Ceiling Vertical displacement is projected along the ceiling; horizontal displacement is constrained Cast and move - Calls PhysicsOperations.MoveUpToNextObstacle to cast the capsule forward by the corrected displacement, move the character to the hit point (or the full distance if nothing was hit), and update contact information. To customize how collisions are resolved, see Custom Collision Response. Step Detection When a wall contact is detected, the default Move() checks whether it could be a step: The character must be in contact with a surface The slope must exceed MaxSlope The character must be moving into the slope The contact height must be below MaxStepHeight If all conditions are met, PhysicsOperations.TryStep attempts to move the character up and over the step. 5. SnapToGround After all collision resolution is complete, the system performs a downward capsule cast to detect the ground surface below the character. This ensures the character stays grounded when walking down slopes or stairs, rather than becoming airborne for a frame. The snap distance is computed by your context's ComputeGroundSnappingDistance method. The default implementation derives it from the character's horizontal speed and the max-slope angle, the current contact slope, and any inherited platform vertical velocity, floored at the max step height — so faster characters on steeper terrain check further. Override this method on your context's partial struct when your game needs a different adhesion policy. If a ground surface is found within the snap distance, the character's position is adjusted downward and the contact information is updated. 6. InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity If the character is standing on a dynamic body (kinematic or fully-simulated), this step computes the displacement and rotation the character inherits from that body's motion velocity. The displacement is applied to the character's position in the same frame. The inherited velocities are stored in: baseContext.PlatformHorizontalVelocity baseContext.PlatformVerticalVelocity These are available immediately - for example, a jumping state's OnEnterState (called during EvaluateTransition in the same frame) can read PlatformHorizontalVelocity to preserve momentum when jumping off a platform. The position adjustment from platform movement is applied automatically, which is why you should never add platform velocity manually in OnIntegrateState. 7. EvaluateTransition The final step evaluates all [LocomotionTransition] structs registered for the current state. By this point: The character has moved to its final position All contacts are resolved and up-to-date Platform inheritance is computed The source generator dispatches to each transition's ShouldTransition method in the order determined by [EvaluateBefore]/[EvaluateAfter] attributes. The first matching transition wins. The generator automatically handles calling OnExitState on the current state and OnEnterState on the new state. Next Steps Writing Custom States - How to implement each lifecycle method Physics Configuration - Tuning the physics profile Recipe: Override a Pipeline Step - Customize individual steps Recipe: Customize Collision Response - Custom behavior in the collide-and-slide loop

manual/extending.html.title: Extending the Package | MGM Character Controller
manual/extending.html.summary: Extending the Package The MGM Character Controller is designed to be extended without modifying the package source. This page covers common extension points and patterns. Extension Points 1. Custom States The most common extension. Add new movement behaviors (wall running, swimming, climbing, dashing) by creating new state structs and adding them to your state enum. See Writing Custom States for the full guide. 2. Custom Profiles Your ILocomotionProfile struct can contain any unmanaged data. Add fields for new gameplay parameters: [Serializable] public partial struct MyProfile : ILocomotionProfile { public MovingProfile Moving; public FallingProfile Falling; public JumpingProfile Jumping; // Custom extension public SwimmingProfile Swimming; public DashProfile Dash; public WallRunProfile WallRun; } Each sub-profile is a plain struct with configuration fields. The data is baked into a blob asset, so add corresponding fields to your LocomotionProfileAsset and BuildBlobAsset method. 3. Custom Context Your context struct can include additional computed properties and helper methods: public partial struct MyContext : ILocomotionContext<MyProfile, MyInput, MyStateData> { public BaseLocomotionContext BaseContext; public MyStateData StateData; // Standard interface properties... // Custom helpers public bool IsUnderwater => BaseContext.CharacterPosition.Position.y < WaterLevel; public bool WantsToMove => Input.MovementMagnitude > math.EPSILON; public bool CanDash => StateData.DashCooldown <= 0; // Custom ground snap for swimming (no ground snap when submerged) public void ComputeGroundSnappingDistance(in MyProfile profile, out float distance) { if (IsUnderwater) { distance = 0; // No ground snapping while swimming return; } // Normal ground snap calculation... } } 4. Custom StateData Add per-state persistent data for any state-specific tracking: public partial struct MyStateData : IComponentData { public JumpData JumpData; public float DashCooldown; public float WallRunTimer; public float3 WallNormal; // Remembered from wall run entry } State data persists across frames and state transitions. Clean it up in OnEnterState or OnExitState as appropriate. 5. Custom Input Add input channels for new actions: public partial struct MyInput : ICharacterLocomotionInput<MyInput> { public float3 Movement; public float JumpTrigger; public float DashTrigger; // New action public float InteractTrigger; // New action public void ApplyInputsToCharacter(in MyInput playerInputs) { Movement = playerInputs.Movement; JumpTrigger += playerInputs.JumpTrigger; // Accumulate triggers DashTrigger += playerInputs.DashTrigger; InteractTrigger += playerInputs.InteractTrigger; } } Remember to read the new inputs in your PlayerInputAsset subclass and consume triggers in your state logic. 6. Custom Ground Snapping Override ComputeGroundSnappingDistance on your context to control when and how far the character snaps to the ground: public void ComputeGroundSnappingDistance(in MyProfile profile, out float distance) { // Disable ground snapping while jumping upward if (StateData.CurrentState == MyStates.Jumping && math.dot(BaseContext.VerticalVelocity, -BaseContext.GravityDirection) > 0) { distance = 0; return; } // Default calculation var slopeDistance = math.length(BaseContext.HorizontalVelocity * BaseContext.TimeStep) * math.tan(math.radians(CharacterPhysicsProfile.MaxSlope)); distance = math.max(CharacterPhysicsProfile.MaxStepHeight, slopeDistance); } 7. Custom Collision Response Override OnResolveStateCollisions to add custom behavior when the character hits something: public void OnResolveStateCollisions(ref MyContext ctx) { BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ctx.BaseContext; baseContext.Move(); // Custom: bounce off trampolines if (baseContext.IsGroundingContact && HasTrampolineTag(baseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO.Entity)) { baseContext.VerticalVelocity = -baseContext.VerticalVelocity * 1.5f; } ctx.BaseContext = baseContext; } 8. Custom Systems You can add systems that modify locomotion components at any point in the pipeline: [UpdateInGroup(typeof(FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup))] [UpdateBefore(typeof(MyLocomotionSystem))] partial struct GravityZoneSystem : ISystem { public void OnUpdate(ref SystemState state) { foreach (var gravity in SystemAPI.Query<RefRW<LocomotionGravity>>() .WithAll<InGravityZone>()) { gravity.ValueRW.Gravity = new float3(0, -4.9f, 0); // Half gravity } } } Customizing the Execution Pipeline Each step in the execution loop is a default interface method (DIM) on ILocomotionStateMachine. You can override any of them on your state machine's partial struct to replace or wrap the default behavior. The source generator produces a partial struct for your state machine (e.g., MyStateMachine). Because it is partial, you can add a second partial declaration that overrides any DIM: public partial struct MyStateMachine { public void Integrate(ref MyStateMachine stateMachine, ref MyContext context) { // Skip movement entirely when crushed if (context.BaseContext.OverlapState == OverlapState.Crush) return; // Otherwise run the default per-state integration stateMachine.IntegratePerState(ref context); } } Overridable Pipeline Methods Method Override to... Execute Replace the entire execution loop HandleExternalImpulses Custom impulse filtering or scaling Integrate Add pre/post integration logic SolveOverlaps Custom overlap resolution CollideAndSlide Custom collision iteration SnapToGround Custom ground adhesion InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity Custom platform riding behavior EvaluateTransition Add pre/post transition logic Note IntegratePerState, ResolveCollisionPerState, and EvaluateTransitionPerState are generated by the source generator (switch dispatches to per-state methods). They are not intended to be overridden directly. See The Execution Loop for the ordering and data flow between these steps. Customizing the Locomotion System The source generator creates a partial interface I{Prefix}LocomotionSystem that inherits from ILocomotionSystem<...>. The generated system struct implements this interface with DIM lifecycle methods that you can override. To customize, add your own partial interface declaration: public partial interface IMyLocomotionSystem { void ILocomotionSystem<MyStateMachine, MyStates, MyContext, MyProfile, MyInput, MyStateData> .OnLocomotionSystemUpdate( ref LocomotionJobData jobData, ref EntityQuery query, ref SystemState state) { if (query.IsEmptyIgnoreFilter) return; jobData = jobData.Update(ref state); // Schedule single-threaded instead of parallel (useful for debugging) state.Dependency = ScheduleLocomotionJob( state.Dependency, state.WorldUnmanaged.Time.DeltaTime, jobData, query, jobData.GetPhysicsWorldSingleton()); } } Overridable System Lifecycle Methods Method Override to... OnLocomotionSystemCreate Add RequireForUpdate, custom query filters, rate manager setup OnLocomotionSystemUpdate Use single-threaded scheduling, add conditional skip, integrate rate manager OnLocomotionSystemDestroy Custom resource cleanup Note The default DIM implementations use ref parameters instead of SystemAPI because Unity's source generator cannot patch call sites in code emitted by the package's source generator (both run in parallel). Your own partial interface overrides can use SystemAPI since they are visible to Unity's generator. DIM Customization Reference Complete reference of all default interface methods across the package: Interface.Method Override to... ILocomotionState.OnEnterState Initialize state-specific data on entry ILocomotionState.OnIntegrateState Custom movement logic per state ILocomotionState.OnExitState Clean up state-specific data on exit ILocomotionState.OnResolveStateCollisions Custom collision response per state ILocomotionContext.ComputeGroundSnappingDistance Speed-dependent or state-dependent snap distance ILocomotionStateMachine.Execute Replace the entire execution loop ILocomotionStateMachine.HandleExternalImpulses Custom impulse handling ILocomotionStateMachine.Integrate Pre/post integration logic ILocomotionStateMachine.SolveOverlaps Custom overlap resolution ILocomotionStateMachine.CollideAndSlide Custom collision loop ILocomotionStateMachine.SnapToGround Custom ground adhesion ILocomotionStateMachine.InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity Custom platform riding ILocomotionStateMachine.EvaluateTransition Pre/post transition logic ILocomotionSystem.OnLocomotionSystemCreate Custom system initialization ILocomotionSystem.OnLocomotionSystemUpdate Custom scheduling strategy ILocomotionSystem.OnLocomotionSystemDestroy Custom resource cleanup ICharacterLocomotionInput.ApplyInputsToCharacter Accumulate/merge inputs between fixed updates Multiple State Machines You can have multiple independent state machine types in the same project. For example: GroundLocomotionStates - Walking, running, jumping, falling VehicleStates - Driving, braking, boosting, airborne SwimmingStates - Surface, submerged, diving Each has its own enum, context, profile, input, state data, and generated systems. They are completely independent. To switch a character between state machines, you would need to add/remove the relevant components (the state machine component, input, profile, state data). This is an advanced pattern that involves structural entity changes. Working with the Source Generator The Roslyn source generator reads attributes on your anchor struct and state structs and generates: State machine component with dispatch logic Input reader system ISystem lifecycle methods (OnCreate, OnUpdate, OnDestroy) on your locomotion system The generator source is at SourceGenerator/SrcGenProj~/. To modify the generated code patterns: Edit StateMachineSourceGenerator.cs Build with dotnet build from the SrcGenProj~ directory The DLL is copied to SourceGenerator/ and picked up by Unity Warning Modifying the source generator affects all state machines in the project. Test thoroughly. Creating Composite Characters For characters that need both ECS locomotion and complex visual hierarchies: The Locomotor entity carries all physics and state machine components A Model entity follows the Locomotor via CharacterFollower The Model's GameObject can have child objects with Animators, particle systems, audio sources The CharacterFollowerAuthoring links the model to the locomotor during baking. At runtime, the CharacterFollowerSystem syncs the transform. To spawn the composition together at runtime with cross-entity references remapped, place all three authorings under a single empty bundle-root GameObject and attach Unity's LinkedEntityGroupAuthoring to that root. Performance Considerations Scaling to Many Characters The locomotion job runs in parallel across chunks. To maximize throughput: Keep all characters with the same archetype (same component set) Use shared colliders (avoid ForceUniqueColliderAuthoring unless needed) Profile shared blob assets (all characters referencing the same profile share memory) Only enable debug visualization on characters you are actively investigating Burst Compilation State methods run inside a Burst-compiled job, so they must be Burst-compatible. Common mistakes that prevent Burst compilation: Using string or List<T> types Calling managed virtual methods (DIM lifecycle methods are dispatched by the source generator, not via virtual dispatch) Accessing GameObject or MonoBehaviour APIs Using Debug.Log (use [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] guards) Profiling Use Unity's Profiler to identify bottlenecks: The locomotion job appears as LocomotionJob in the Jobs timeline Per-stage profiler markers are static fields on ILocomotionStateMachine, gated by [Conditional("ENABLE_LOCOMOTION_PROFILER")] via ProfilerMarkerExtensions Next Steps Getting Started - Set up your first character Architecture Overview - Understand the full system design Writing Custom States - Implement new movement behaviors Recipe: Override a Pipeline Step - Step-by-step pipeline override Recipe: Run Multiple State Machines - Independent state machines in one project Best Practices - Recommended patterns and anti-patterns

manual/fixed-step-rate.html.title: Fixed Step Rate | MGM Character Controller
manual/fixed-step-rate.html.summary:
Fixed Step Rate The locomotion job runs inside Unity's FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup, so the fixed timestep directly controls how often characters simulate. The package lets you author that rate as data instead of hardcoding it in a bootstrap: place a FixedStepRateAuthoring component in a sub-scene and the rate is baked and applied automatically. How It Works flowchart LR A["FixedStepRateAuthoring
MonoBehaviour in a SubScene
FixedUpdatesPerSecond (Hz)"] B["FixedStepRate
singleton component
Timestep (seconds)"] C["ApplyFixedStepRateSystem
InitializationSystemGroup
runs every frame"] D["FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup
.Timestep"] A -- "baked" --> B B -- "read" --> C C -- "write" --> D FixedStepRateAuthoring Place this on a GameObject inside a sub-scene. It exposes Fixed Updates Per Second (1-240 Hz, default 60) and bakes it into a FixedStepRate singleton as a timestep in seconds (1 / Hz). FixedStepRate The singleton component holding the fixed timestep in seconds (e.g. 1/120 ≈ 0.0083 for 120 Hz). ApplyFixedStepRateSystem Runs in InitializationSystemGroup and only updates while a FixedStepRate singleton exists. Every frame it copies the singleton's Timestep onto the FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup. Running every frame (rather than once) means you can tweak the value live while the sub-scene is open in the Editor. Changing the Rate at Runtime Because the system re-applies the singleton every frame, changing the rate at runtime means writing the singleton (writing only the system group's Timestep would be overwritten on the next frame). The BehaviorShowCase sample's timestep slider does both, so the change also takes effect on the current frame: using var query = em.CreateEntityQuery(ComponentType.ReadWrite()); if (!query.IsEmpty) query.SetSingleton(new FixedStepRate { Timestep = timestep }); Next Steps The Execution Loop - What runs each fixed update Samples - The BehaviorShowCase timestep slider in action

manual/getting-started.html.title: Getting Started | MGM Character Controller
manual/getting-started.html.summary: Getting Started This guide walks you through creating your first character from scratch using the editor scaffolding tool. If you just want to see the package working quickly, start with the Quickstart instead (uses the pre-built sample). Prerequisites MGM Character Controller installed and compiling (Installation) Basic familiarity with Unity ECS concepts (entities, components, systems, baking). If you are new to ECS, review Unity's Entities documentation first. Project Setup Your project needs a sub-scene with physics enabled. The package relies on Unity.Physics for all collision detection and does not use the legacy physics system. Create or open a scene Add a Sub Scene (right-click in Hierarchy > New Sub Scene) Ensure the sub-scene has a Physics Step component (automatically present in most setups) Add colliders to your environment (floor, walls, etc.) Creating Your First Character The fastest way to get started is to use the built-in scaffolding tool: Step 1: Generate the State Machine In the Project window, right-click on the folder where you want to create your state machine Select Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller > StateMachine Name the folder (e.g., MyCharacter) Press Enter The tool generates a minimal folder structure with the anchor file. Everything else is source-generated at compile time: MyCharacter/ ├── Runtime/ │ ├── mycharacter.runtime.asmdef # Auto-generated assembly definition │ └── MyCharacterStateMachine.cs # Anchor struct with [LocomotionStateMachine] attribute └── Authoring/ └── mycharacter.authoring.asmdef # Auto-generated assembly definition After compilation, the source generator produces all remaining types in memory (context, state enum, profile, input, state data, authoring components, locomotion system, input reader system). You then add states, transitions, and data structs via the Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller sub-menus. Step 2: Create the Profile Asset In the Project window, right-click Select the Create menu item for your character profile asset (the menu path is generated for you) Configure movement speed, jump force, gravity multiplier, and other parameters in the Inspector Step 3: Create the Input Asset Right-click in the Project window Select the Create menu item for your player input asset Assign your Input Action References for movement and jump Step 4: Set Up the Character Prefab Create a new GameObject in your sub-scene Add the generated Character Locomotor Authoring component Assign your Profile Asset Configure the Physics Profile (capsule height, radius, mass, max slope, etc.) Step 5: Set Up the Player Prefab The Player is a separate concept from the Character. Players own input and control one or more characters. Create a GameObject in the sub-scene (it is baked into a Player entity) Add the generated Player Character Authoring component Assign the Controlled Character (the Locomotor's authoring component), the Input Asset, and the Player GO Prefab (a regular GameObject prefab containing camera and input components, saved outside the sub-scene) Step 6: Enter Play Mode Press Play. Your character should respond to input and interact with the physics environment. If the character falls through the floor, verify that: Your floor has a physics collider The character's collision layers (BelongsTo and CollidesWith) are configured correctly The sub-scene is loaded Importing the Sample The package includes a SinglePlayerSample that demonstrates a complete setup with five states (Idling, Moving, Jumping, Falling, Sliding), a camera rig, and moving platforms. To study the sample: Import Single Player Sample from Window > Package Manager > Samples, then navigate to Assets/Samples/MGM Character Controller/0.8.0/Single Player Sample/ Open the scene Scenes/SinglePlayerSample.unity Review the scripts in Scripts/SimpleCharacter/ for a complete reference implementation Tip The sample is the best resource for understanding how all the pieces connect. Read it alongside this documentation. Next Steps Architecture Overview - Understand the entity types and system design The Execution Loop - Learn what happens each physics tick Writing Custom States - Add new movement behaviors Samples - Study the sample code in detail Troubleshooting - Common setup issues and fixes

manual/hybrid-layer.html.title: Hybrid GameObject Layer | MGM Character Controller
manual/hybrid-layer.html.summary: Hybrid GameObject Layer The Hybrid layer bridges the gap between ECS entities and GameObjects. It enables characters driven by Burst-compiled ECS logic to have animated 3D models, particle effects, audio sources, and cameras, all of which require MonoBehaviour and GameObject APIs. Why a Hybrid Layer? Burst-compiled jobs cannot touch GameObjects, Cameras, Animators, or any managed Unity API. But games need these for rendering, animation, audio, and UI. The hybrid layer solves this by: Running all locomotion logic in pure ECS (fast, parallel, Burst-compatible) Syncing entity transforms to GameObjects each frame via Burst-compiled jobs using TransformAccessArray Letting MonoBehaviours on those GameObjects react to position/rotation changes This means you get the performance of ECS for simulation and the convenience of GameObjects for presentation. Assembly The hybrid layer lives in the WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Hybrid assembly, which references the Runtime assembly. Your game code can reference Hybrid if it needs to interact with the bridge systems. Core Types EntityGameObject (MonoBehaviour) Attached to a GameObject that is linked to an ECS entity. It stores the Entity and World references and registers/unregisters the GameObject's Transform with the singleton transform sync system. When the GameObject is destroyed, its OnDestroy method automatically handles entity cleanup to prevent dangling references. GameObjectEntity (Managed Component) A managed class implementing IComponentData that stores a GameObject Prefab reference, allowing systems to look up the GameObject prefab from the entity side. Because it holds a managed reference, it cannot be used in Burst-compiled jobs. EntityGoCleanup (Managed Cleanup Component) A managed class implementing ICleanupComponentData that stores the GameObject Instance. The EntityGoCleanupSystem processes these to ensure GameObjects are properly disposed when their entities are destroyed. Systems EntityGoInitialisationSystem Runs when new entities with GameObjectEntity components appear. It: Instantiates the referenced GameObject prefab Attaches an EntityGameObject MonoBehaviour to link it back to the entity Registers the transform for syncing EntityGoTransformSyncSystem A system that maintains a static registry of (Entity, Transform) pairs. Each frame, after all ECS jobs complete, it copies LocalToWorld from each registered entity to the corresponding GameObject's Transform. The sync is performed by a Burst-compiled IJobParallelForTransform scheduled via TransformAccessArray, allowing it to run on worker threads rather than the main thread. EntityGoCleanupSystem Processes entities with the EntityGoCleanup component. When an entity is destroyed, this system ensures the associated GameObject is also destroyed, preventing orphaned GameObjects in the scene. EntityGoEditorPreviewSystem (Editor Only) Provides editor-time preview of entity-linked GameObjects. This allows you to see the visual representation in the Scene view without entering Play mode. Character Follower The CharacterFollower component is an ECS component added to "model" entities. It stores a reference to the Locomotor entity that the model should follow. The CharacterFollowerSystem runs each frame and copies the Locomotor's position and rotation to the model entity. The model entity then has its transform synced to the associated GameObject by EntityGoTransformSyncSystem. This two-hop chain (Locomotor -> Model Entity -> GameObject) ensures: The Locomotor runs in parallel with no GameObject dependencies The Model entity can apply visual offsets or smoothing The GameObject receives the final visual transform Player GameObject Management PlayerGoManagerSystem This system manages the lifecycle of player GameObjects: Spawn: When a new Player entity appears with a PlayerGameObjectPrefab but no PlayerGameObjectInstance, the system instantiates the prefab and stores the instance reference Destroy: When a Player entity is destroyed, the system destroys the associated GameObject The player GameObject typically contains: A Camera component A CinemachineBrain for camera blending A PlayerInput component for input handling A PlayerGoAuthoring with references to the camera, camera target, and follow strategy CameraRigFollowControlledCharacterSystem Ensures the player's camera rig follows the controlled character. It maintains a Singleton component with registered player entities and camera transforms, then copies each player entity's LocalToWorld position to the corresponding camera rig transform. DestructionManager A MonoBehaviour that manages delayed destruction of GameObjects. It invokes a configurable UnityEvent before destroying the GameObject after an optional delay. Entity cleanup is handled separately by EntityGameObject.OnDestroy(). For a step-by-step setup guide, see Recipe: Set Up a Hybrid Character. Next Steps Architecture Overview - How the entity types relate Input System - How player input flows through the system Integration: Animation - Connecting an Animator to a hybrid character Integration: Cinemachine - Camera setup on player GameObjects

manual/input-system.html.title: Input System | MGM Character Controller
manual/input-system.html.summary:
Input System The MGM Character Controller separates input reading from input consumption. This design supports multiple input sources (keyboard, gamepad, AI, network), handles frame rate differences between Update and FixedUpdate, and works cleanly with Unity's new Input System. The guaranteed input behavior is specified as INP-1–INP-4 in the behavior specification shipped with the package (Documentation~/spec/). Architecture Input flows through three layers: flowchart LR subgraph L1["1. Read"] A["PlayerInputAsset
MonoBehaviour · ScriptableObject
Reads hardware input
Update rate"] end subgraph L2["2. Accumulate"] B["ICharacterLocomotionInput
ECS component
ApplyInputsToCharacter()
Update rate"] end subgraph L3["3. Consume"] C["State logic
Burst job
Reads TInput on context
FixedUpdate rate"] end A -- "ReadInputsFromAsset(out TInput)" --> B B -- "generated InputReaderSystem" --> C Why Three Layers? Frame rate mismatch: Unity's Update loop runs at variable rate (e.g., 60-144 fps), but FixedUpdate runs at a fixed rate (e.g., 50 fps). If a player presses Jump during a frame where no FixedUpdate runs, that press must not be lost. The accumulation layer ensures trigger inputs survive until the next fixed step. Burst compatibility: PlayerInputAsset is a ScriptableObject that touches MonoBehaviour APIs (Camera, PlayerInput, Input System). These cannot run inside Burst jobs. The separation allows the managed-code layer to read input and the Burst-compiled layer to consume it. Multiple input sources: By abstracting input behind ICharacterLocomotionInput, you can swap the input source without changing any state logic. A keyboard player, a gamepad player, and an AI agent all write to the same TInput component. PlayerInputAsset PlayerInputAsset is an abstract ScriptableObject that you subclass to define how hardware input maps to your input struct. [CreateAssetMenu(menuName = "My Game/Player Input Asset")] public class MyPlayerInputAsset : PlayerInputAsset { public InputActionReference MovementAction; public InputActionReference JumpAction; Camera _camera; PlayerInput _playerInput; public override void ReadInputsFromAsset(out MyInput inputs) { // Read raw input var moveRaw = _playerInput.actions[MovementAction.name].ReadValue(); // Convert to world-space relative to camera Transform cam = _camera.transform; float3 worldMove = cam.forward * moveRaw.y + cam.right * moveRaw.x; worldMove -= math.projectsafe(worldMove, math.up()); // Remove vertical component inputs.Movement = math.normalizesafe(worldMove); // Read trigger inputs.JumpTrigger = _playerInput.actions[JumpAction.name].WasPerformedThisFrame() ? 1f : 0f; } public override void InitInputAsset(PlayerGameObjectInstance instance) { var playerGo = instance.Instance.Value; _camera = playerGo.GetComponent().Camera; _playerInput = playerGo.GetComponent(); _playerInput.ActivateInput(); } } Key points ReadInputsFromAsset is called every Update frame (not FixedUpdate). Return a fresh TInput each call. InitInputAsset is called once when the player is instantiated. Use it to cache references to the camera, PlayerInput, and any other managed objects. The asset is instantiated per player at runtime (ScriptableObject.Instantiate), so each player gets their own cached references. Multiple players on the same machine each have their own copy. Camera-Relative Input Most 3D games convert 2D stick/keyboard input to world-space movement relative to the camera. The pattern is: Read the 2D input vector Multiply by the camera's forward and right vectors Project onto the horizontal plane (remove the gravity-axis component) Normalize This ensures "push up on the stick" always means "move away from the camera," regardless of camera angle. ICharacterLocomotionInput Your input struct must implement this interface: public struct MyInput : ICharacterLocomotionInput { public float3 Movement; public float JumpTrigger; public void ApplyInputsToCharacter(in MyInput playerInputs) { // Continuous inputs: overwrite with latest value Movement = playerInputs.Movement; // Trigger inputs: ACCUMULATE, don't overwrite JumpTrigger += playerInputs.JumpTrigger; } } Input Accumulation The critical distinction is between continuous and trigger inputs: Type Example Behavior Why Continuous Movement direction, aim angle Overwrite each frame Only the latest value matters Trigger Jump press, fire button Accumulate across frames A press during a non-FixedUpdate frame must not be lost If you overwrite JumpTrigger instead of accumulating it, and the player presses Jump during a frame where no FixedUpdate runs, the press is silently discarded. Consuming Triggers In your state's OnIntegrateState, after reading the trigger value, reset it to zero: public void OnIntegrateState(ref MyContext ctx) { if (ctx.Input.JumpTrigger > 0) { // Apply jump Jump(ref ctx); } // Consume the trigger MyInput input = ctx.Input; input.JumpTrigger = 0; ctx.Input = input; } Generated Input Reader System The source generator creates an input reader system that: Runs each Update frame (not FixedUpdate) For each player, calls PlayerInputAsset.ReadInputsFromAsset to get raw input For each character controlled by that player, calls ICharacterLocomotionInput.ApplyInputsToCharacter to write to the ECS component You never need to write or modify this system. It is produced automatically from your [LocomotionStateMachine] annotation. AI and Network Input Because input is just an ECS component, you can drive characters from any source: AI Input Create a system that writes directly to the TInput component without going through PlayerInputAsset: [BurstCompile] partial struct AIInputSystem : ISystem { [BurstCompile] public void OnUpdate(ref SystemState state) { foreach (var (input, transform) in SystemAPI.Query, RefRO>() .WithAll()) { // AI decision-making logic input.ValueRW.Movement = ComputeAIMovement(transform.ValueRO); input.ValueRW.JumpTrigger = ShouldJump() ? 1f : 0f; } } } Network Input For networked games, the client sends input to the server, which writes it to the TInput component. The locomotion job is Burst-compiled and runs at a fixed timestep. Networking is not a shipped capability of this package: no Netcode integration is provided, cross-client/server determinism has not been verified, and you own the replication and reconciliation strategy. For the current state of networking prerequisites and the planned (not yet built) network sample, see the network sample plan in the product docs. Cinemachine Integration The sample uses Cinemachine through the Player (GO) prefab: the virtual camera and CinemachineBrain are pre-wired in the prefab and follow the CameraTarget transform that CameraRigFollowControlledCharacterSystem keeps on the character. No Cinemachine code lives in the input asset - the sample's SimpleCharacterPlayerInputAsset only caches the Camera and CameraTarget transforms (via PlayerGoAuthoring) to compute camera-relative movement. Because the whole camera rig lives on the per-player prefab instance, each player in a local multiplayer setup gets their own camera pipeline. Next Steps Hybrid GameObject Layer - How player GameObjects are managed Writing Custom States - Consuming input in state logic Integration: Cinemachine - Camera setup with Cinemachine Recipe: Switch to AI Input - Drive characters from AI systems

manual/install.html.title: Installation | MGM Character Controller
manual/install.html.summary: Installation This page covers installing the MGM Character Controller package and verifying that everything is working. Prerequisites Unity 6000.3 or later A project configured for DOTS (Entities, Unity.Physics, Burst, Jobs) If you are new to Unity ECS, review Unity's Entities documentation first. You do not need to be an ECS expert, but you should understand the basic concepts of entities, components, systems, and baking. Install from the Asset Store Purchase or download the package from the Unity Asset Store Open your Unity project Go to Window > Package Manager Select My Assets in the dropdown Find MGM Character Controller and click Import Install from a Local Folder Open your Unity project Go to Window > Package Manager Click the + button and select Add package from disk... Navigate to the package.json file inside the package folder Click Open Install from a Git URL Open Window > Package Manager Click + > Add package from git URL... Enter the repository URL Verify Installation After installation, confirm the package is working: Open Window > Package Manager Find MGM Character Controller in the package list Verify the version shows 0.8.0 Check the Console for any compilation errors If you see errors related to missing Entities or Physics packages, install the required dependencies: Package Minimum Version com.unity.entities 1.3.9 com.unity.physics 1.3.8 com.unity.burst 1.8.18 com.unity.collections 2.5.4 com.unity.mathematics 1.3.2 Next Step Continue to the Quickstart to see a character running in minutes.

manual/integrations/animation.html.title: Integration: Animation | MGM Character Controller
manual/integrations/animation.html.summary: Integration: Animation Characters driven by the MGM Character Controller use a separate Model entity with an attached GameObject for rendering and animation. The Animator component lives on this GameObject, not on the ECS entity. Architecture Locomotor Entity (ECS) → CharacterFollower → Model Entity (ECS) → GameObject (Animator) The Locomotor entity runs state machine logic in Burst jobs The Model entity follows the Locomotor via CharacterFollowerSystem The Model's GameObject gets its transform synced via EntityGoTransformSyncSystem A MonoBehaviour on the GameObject reads entity state and drives the Animator Setup 1. Create the model GameObject In the sub-scene: Create a child GameObject with your character mesh and Animator Add a CharacterFollowerAuthoring component Set the Locomotor field to reference the character's Locomotor authoring component 2. Create an animation bridge MonoBehaviour Since Burst jobs cannot touch the Animator, you need a MonoBehaviour bridge that reads ECS state and sets Animator parameters: public class LocomotionAnimationBridge : MonoBehaviour { Animator _animator; EntityGameObject _entityLink; // Animator parameter hashes static readonly int SpeedHash = Animator.StringToHash("Speed"); static readonly int IsGroundedHash = Animator.StringToHash("IsGrounded"); static readonly int IsJumpingHash = Animator.StringToHash("IsJumping"); void Awake() { _animator = GetComponent<Animator>(); _entityLink = GetComponent<EntityGameObject>(); } void LateUpdate() { if (_entityLink == null || !_entityLink.IsValid) return; // Read entity data from the ECS world var entityManager = World.DefaultGameObjectInjectionWorld.EntityManager; var entity = _entityLink.Entity; // Read velocity for speed parameter if (entityManager.HasComponent<LocomotionVelocity>(entity)) { var velocity = entityManager.GetComponentData<LocomotionVelocity>(entity); _animator.SetFloat(SpeedHash, math.length(velocity.Value)); } // Read contact for grounded state if (entityManager.HasComponent<LocomotionContact>(entity)) { var contact = entityManager.GetComponentData<LocomotionContact>(entity); _animator.SetBool(IsGroundedHash, contact.ContactType == ContactType.Ground); } } } 3. Attach to the model GameObject Add LocomotionAnimationBridge to the same GameObject that has the Animator. The EntityGameObject component is added automatically by the hybrid layer during initialization. State-Aware Animation To read the current state machine state, you need access to the generated state machine component. Since this is a generic type, you can either: Option A: Use a managed component or shared data structure to expose the current state to MonoBehaviours. Option B: Create a system that writes animation-relevant data to a dedicated "animation data" component readable from the bridge. Option B is recommended because it keeps the main thread work minimal: public struct AnimationData : IComponentData { public float Speed; public bool IsGrounded; public bool IsJumping; public bool IsFalling; } [UpdateAfter(typeof(MyLocomotionSystem))] partial struct AnimationDataSystem : ISystem { public void OnUpdate(ref SystemState state) { foreach (var (animData, velocity, contact) in SystemAPI.Query<RefRW<AnimationData>, RefRO<LocomotionVelocity>, RefRO<LocomotionContact>>()) { animData.ValueRW.Speed = math.length(velocity.ValueRO.Value); animData.ValueRW.IsGrounded = contact.ValueRO.ContactType == ContactType.Ground; } } } Known Caveats Animation is always one frame behind physics because the Animator runs after ECS syncs the transform Root motion is not supported - the Locomotor entity drives position, not the Animator Blending between states should be handled by the Animator Controller, not by the locomotion state machine Next Steps Hybrid GameObject Layer - How entity-to-GameObject sync works Architecture Overview - Locomotor vs Model entity separation

manual/integrations/cinemachine.html.title: Integration: Cinemachine | MGM Character Controller
manual/integrations/cinemachine.html.summary: Integration: Cinemachine The MGM Character Controller works with Cinemachine for third-person (and other) camera setups. The Player prefab holds the camera rig, and the system automatically connects it to the controlled character. Setup 1. Player prefab The Player GO Prefab should contain: A Camera component A CinemachineBrain on the same camera GameObject One or more Cinemachine virtual cameras (e.g., CinemachineCamera for third-person follow) A PlayerGoAuthoring MonoBehaviour with references to the camera and a camera target transform 2. Virtual camera targeting In your PlayerInputAsset.InitInputAsset, connect the virtual cameras to the character's camera target: public override void InitInputAsset(PlayerGameObjectInstance instance) { var playerGo = instance.Instance.Value; var playerGoAuthoring = playerGo.GetComponent<PlayerGoAuthoring>(); _camera = playerGoAuthoring.Camera; _playerInput = playerGo.GetComponent<PlayerInput>(); // Connect Cinemachine cameras to the character's follow target var cameraTarget = playerGoAuthoring.CameraTarget; var virtualCameras = playerGo.GetComponentsInChildren<CinemachineVirtualCameraBase>(); foreach (var vc in virtualCameras) { vc.Follow = cameraTarget; vc.LookAt = cameraTarget; } } 3. Camera target tracking The CameraRigFollowControlledCharacterSystem updates the camera target position to match the controlled character's position each frame. This happens automatically when the Player entity has a ControlledCharacters buffer. 4. Camera-relative input In ReadInputsFromAsset, convert 2D input to world-space relative to the camera: Transform cam = _camera.transform; float3 worldMove = cam.forward * moveRaw.y + cam.right * moveRaw.x; worldMove -= math.projectsafe(worldMove, math.up()); inputs.Movement = math.normalizesafe(worldMove); Local Multiplayer For split-screen setups: Each Player entity gets its own Player GO Prefab instance Each instance has its own Camera + CinemachineBrain CinemachineInputAxisController components should have their PlayerIndex set to match the PlayerInput component's player index The PlayerInputAsset is instantiated per player, so each player caches their own camera reference. Known Caveats The camera target transform is a GameObject synced via CameraRigFollowControlledCharacterSystem, which uses a Burst-compiled IJobParallelForTransform with TransformAccessArray. Camera lag during fast movement can occur if the sync runs after Cinemachine's update. Ensure the sync system runs before Cinemachine evaluates. Next Steps Input System - Camera-relative input in depth Hybrid GameObject Layer - How player GameObjects are managed

manual/moving-platforms.html.title: Moving Platforms | MGM Character Controller
manual/moving-platforms.html.summary: Moving Platforms The MGM Character Controller has built-in support for moving and rotating platforms. Characters standing on platforms automatically inherit their velocity and rotation without any special logic in your state code. The guaranteed platform behavior is specified as PLT-1–PLT-7 in the behavior specification shipped with the package (Documentation~/spec/). How It Works Moving platforms are kinematic physics bodies. The locomotion system detects when a character is grounded on any dynamic body (kinematic or fully-simulated) and automatically computes the displacement and rotation the character should inherit.
