Contact Detection During the SnapToGround step, the system detects that the character is standing on a dynamic body. It records the body index and entity reference in the LocomotionContact component. InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity At the end of the locomotion job, the InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity step reads the body's motion velocity from the physics world and decomposes it into: PlatformHorizontalVelocity - The body's velocity projected onto the horizontal plane PlatformVerticalVelocity - The body's velocity along the gravity axis The displacement is applied to the character's position in the same frame. The platform rotation is applied directly via a twist quaternion computation. The inherited velocities are available immediately in the same frame's EvaluateTransition step (e.g., a jumping state's OnEnterState can read PlatformHorizontalVelocity to preserve momentum when jumping off a platform). Important You should never add platform velocity manually in OnIntegrateState. The system handles it automatically. Adding it yourself would result in double-application, making the character move twice as fast on platforms. Platform Components PlatformMover Stores the movement speed and current waypoint index for track-based platform movement. Updated by the PlatformMovementSystem. Rotor Stores angular velocity for rotating platforms. The system applies the rotation each fixed update. Track Constrains platform motion along a predefined path. The platform loops cyclically through waypoints. For a step-by-step setup guide, see Recipe: Set Up a Moving Platform. PlatformMovementSystem The PlatformMovementSystem runs in the BeforePhysicsSystemGroup and computes the desired linear and angular velocities based on PlatformMover and Rotor components. It writes to the PhysicsVelocity component only - Unity.Physics then integrates those velocities to update the platform's transform during the physics step. Character Behavior on Platforms Standing Still When idle on a platform, the character moves with the platform. If the platform rotates, the character's rotation is updated directly by the InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity step, which extracts the twist (the rotation around the contact surface normal) from the platform's angular motion and applies it to the character's rotation. No state code is involved - the sample's Idling state does nothing in OnIntegrateState. Moving on a Platform When walking on a moving platform, the character's own velocity is additive with the platform's velocity. The character moves relative to the platform surface. Jumping off a Platform When the character jumps, the sample's Jumping.OnEnterState adds PlatformHorizontalVelocity to the character's horizontal velocity: ctx.BaseContext.HorizontalVelocity += ctx.BaseContext.PlatformHorizontalVelocity; This preserves the platform's momentum, so jumping off a fast-moving platform launches the character in the direction the platform was moving. Without this, the character would appear to "snap back" to a standstill mid-air. Platform Push (Overlap Resolution) If a platform moves into the character (e.g., a rising elevator ceiling), the SolveOverlaps step pushes the character out. If the character is trapped between two surfaces (e.g., elevator ceiling and floor), the overlap state transitions through Push -> Pinch -> Crush. When the character is pushed into geometry, the collide-and-slide algorithm can still move it back out because backface collisions are ignored. This means a character that has been shoved inside a wall by a platform can escape by moving away from the wall - the capsule cast will not collide with the interior face of the geometry. Custom Platform Behaviors You can create custom platform movement by writing your own system that modifies the PhysicsVelocity component on platform entities. The locomotion system will automatically handle character inheritance for any dynamic body the character is grounded on. Important Your system must run in BeforePhysicsSystemGroup so that the velocities are set before Unity.Physics integrates them into the platform's transform. For example, a platform that follows a spline: [BurstCompile] [UpdateInGroup(typeof(BeforePhysicsSystemGroup))] partial struct SplinePlatformSystem : ISystem { [BurstCompile] public void OnUpdate(ref SystemState state) { float dt = SystemAPI.Time.fixedDeltaTime; foreach (var (velocity, spline, transform) in SystemAPI.Query<RefRW<PhysicsVelocity>, RefRW<SplineFollower>, RefRO<LocalTransform>>() ) { float3 targetPos = EvaluateSpline(spline.ValueRO, SystemAPI.Time.ElapsedTime); velocity.ValueRW.Linear = (targetPos - transform.ValueRO.Position) / dt; } } } Next Steps The Execution Loop - Understand the platform-related steps Physics Configuration - Platform-relevant physics settings Recipe: Per-Character Gravity - Gravity wells and custom gravity zones

manual/performance.html.title: Performance | MGM Character Controller
manual/performance.html.summary: Performance MGM Character Controller is DOTS-first and built to scale. The simulation hot path is Burst-compiled, runs as parallel IJobChunk jobs, and allocates nothing per tick, so it holds up as character counts grow into the tens of thousands. Rather than lean on a single headline number — which depends heavily on hardware, simulation rate, render path, and scene composition — this page publishes the measured cost across a matrix of simulation rates and crowd sizes, on transparent reference hardware, so you can judge scalability for your own target. Simulation cost matrix Per-frame simulation cost (rendering excluded), measured across simulation frequency and character count. Each cell is the mean cost of one simulation-path frame at a 60 fps render cadence, so a cell is directly comparable to the simulation share of the 16.67 ms 60 fps frame budget. At simulation rate F, a frame runs F/60 fixed ticks. Characters 20 Hz 30 Hz 50 Hz 60 Hz 1 0.13 0.15 0.20 0.21 100 0.30 0.39 0.56 0.64 1 000 0.51 0.65 0.93 1.07 10 000 1.40 1.86 2.92 3.37 20 000 2.31 3.31 5.18 5.93 30 000 3.29 4.68 7.32 8.56 Milliseconds per frame; lower is better. Reading it: at 30 000 characters with a 60 Hz simulation, the controller's simulation costs about 8.6 ms per frame. A full frame including Entity Graphics rendering measures ~9.1 ms median (max ~13.3 ms over 120 frames) — comfortably under the 16.67 ms 60 fps budget, with every measured frame inside budget. Lowering the simulation rate scales the crowd further: the same 30 000 characters at 30 Hz cost about 4.7 ms of simulation per frame, a common choice for very large background populations. Memory: the simulation path allocates 0 bytes per tick at every count in the matrix. The hot path is allocation-free by design (parallel IJobChunk, Burst), so it does not generate per-frame GC pressure at any scale measured here. Reference hardware and configuration CPU AMD Ryzen 9 5950X — 16 cores / 32 threads, 3.4 GHz base RAM 64 GB GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti OS Windows 11 Pro (build 26100) Unity 6000.3.11f1, Burst 1.8.28 (enabled) Config Release code optimization; jobs debugger, native leak detection, and Burst safety checks OFF Measured for 0.8.0 (July 2026) on an otherwise-idle machine. The configuration above is representative of a shipped runtime rather than the editor's debug default (see below). Measurement conditions and honest limits Representative config, still editor. These are Unity editor measurements with Burst enabled, Release code optimization, and the editor safety layers (jobs debugger, native leak detection, Burst safety checks) turned off — close to a shipped IL2CPP player build, but not a standalone build. For reference, the editor's default config (those safety layers ON) runs roughly 40% slower on this workload, so a developer profiling with defaults will see higher numbers; the figures here are the closer-to-shipped ones. Simulation matrix excludes rendering. Rendering a crowd this size is handled by Entity Graphics (instanced batch rendering). The full-loop figure above (30k / 60 Hz ~9.1 ms median) is a separate PlayMode measurement that includes render + present, so it and the sim matrix come from different harnesses and are not simply additive — read the matrix as the sim scalability surface and the full-loop figure as the on-screen frame cost. Terrain-only collision. The measured population collides with the ground, not with each other — the intended locomotion-at-scale scenario. A dense, mutually-colliding crowd is a heavier, different workload. Single-threaded contact stage. The controller's contact-resolution stage is single-threaded, so the largest-tier figures reflect a single-core cap on that stage. Reproducing these numbers The matrix is produced by SimulationFrequencyMatrixTests and the per-tick allocation by SimulationMemoryTests, both EditMode tests over the PerfSpawner scene (Behavior Showcase, Scenes/PerfTests/); the full-loop figure is RenderFrameBudgetTests (PlayMode, -force-d3d11). They record Unity Performance Testing sample groups — view them under Window ▸ Analysis ▸ Performance Test Report. Everything needed to reproduce the numbers is in the editor — no external tooling: Surface the package's test assemblies in the Test Runner by adding the package to "testables" in your project's Packages/manifest.json: "testables": ["wayn.games.mgm.character-controller"]. Import the Behavior Showcase sample (Package Manager ▸ this package ▸ Samples) — it carries the PerfSpawner scene the tests load. Switch the editor to the shipped-representative config by turning the safety layers off: Jobs ▸ Burst ▸ Safety Checks ▸ Off, Jobs ▸ JobsDebugger (uncheck), Jobs ▸ Leak Detection ▸ Off, and set C# code optimization to Release (the debug icon in the editor's bottom-right status bar ▸ Switch to release mode; one recompile follows). With the editor's default config (safety layers on) expect the roughly 40% higher numbers noted above. Run the tests from Window ▸ General ▸ Test Runner (EditMode for the matrix and memory tests, PlayMode for the full-loop figure). These are measurement surfaces, not pass/fail gates: they characterize cost, they do not enforce a budget.

manual/physics-configuration.html.title: Physics Configuration | MGM Character Controller
manual/physics-configuration.html.summary: Physics Configuration The CharacterPhysicsProfile defines the physical properties of the character's collision capsule and how it interacts with the world. This page explains each parameter, its effect, and how to tune it. CharacterPhysicsProfile Fields Capsule Geometry Field Type Description CapsuleHeight float Total height of the collision capsule from bottom to top, in world units. The capsule's bottom sphere sits at y = CapsuleRadius and the top sphere at y = CapsuleHeight - CapsuleRadius. CapsuleRadius float Radius of both hemisphere caps. Also determines the minimum width of the character. Default: 0.5. The capsule geometry directly affects: Which gaps the character can fit through How close the character can get to walls Step detection (contact height relative to capsule bottom) Mass and Forces Field Type Description Mass float Weight of the character. Used for collision response calculations when the character collides with dynamic rigid bodies. Higher mass means the character pushes objects more. MassToDynamic float Multiplier applied to all impulses the character exerts on dynamic bodies during collision response. Movement Limits Field Type Description MaxSlope float Maximum slope angle (in degrees) the character can walk up. Surfaces steeper than this are treated as walls. Typical values: 45-60 degrees. MaxStepHeight float Maximum height (in world units) of obstacles the character can automatically step over. Typical values: 0.3-0.5. MaxBounce int Maximum number of collide-and-slide iterations per frame. Each bounce allows the character to redirect along a surface it hits. Higher values handle more complex geometry (corners, narrow corridors) but cost more. Default: 3. The slope-walking and step-up behavior these limits govern is guaranteed as LOC-2 and LOC-3 in the behavior specification shipped with the package (Documentation~/spec/). Collision Layers Field Type Description BelongsTo LayerMask The physics layer(s) this character belongs to. Other colliders check this to decide if they can collide with the character. CollidesWith LayerMask The physics layer(s) this character tests against. The character only detects collisions with colliders on these layers. To make characters ignore each other, put them on a layer that does not appear in other characters' CollidesWith mask. To make characters collide with each other, include the character layer in both masks. Collision Tolerance Field Type Description CollisionTolerance float Skin thickness for all collision queries. This is the distance at which the system considers two surfaces "in contact." Decrease for tighter collision response; increase if you observe jitter or tunneling. Defaults to CollisionWorld.DefaultCollisionTolerance. Interpolation Field Type Description InterpolationMode enum Interpolated enables Unity.Physics graphical smoothing between fixed updates, producing smoother visual movement. NotInterpolated updates the transform directly each fixed step, which can appear jittery at low fixed rates but is simpler to debug. Default Values The static CharacterPhysicsProfile.Default property provides sensible starting values: CharacterPhysicsProfile.Default = new CharacterPhysicsProfile { MaxBounce = 3, CapsuleRadius = 0.5f, CapsuleHeight = 2f, BelongsTo = 1, // Layer 0 (Default) CollidesWith = ~0, // All layers CollisionTolerance = CollisionWorld.DefaultCollisionTolerance }; Collision Response The character's capsule collider is created with CollisionResponsePolicy.CollideRaiseCollisionEvents. This means: The collider participates in collision detection Collision events are raised, allowing CharacterContactSystem to intercept contacts However, CollideRaiseCollisionEvents alone would still let Unity.Physics solve the contact normally. The package prevents this by setting JacobianFlags.Disabled on every contact that involves a character inside CharacterContactSystem. This disables the physics solver's constraint for that contact, giving the locomotion job full control over the character's movement. The system then records the contact data (penetration depth, surface normal, velocity) for use by the locomotion pipeline's SolveOverlaps and HandleExternalImpulses steps. Shared vs Unique Colliders By default, capsule colliders are shared across entities with identical geometry and filter settings. This saves memory when you have many characters with the same shape. If you need a unique collider per entity (e.g., for runtime shape modification), add a ForceUniqueColliderAuthoring component to the character's authoring GameObject. Tuning Guide Character walks through walls Increase MaxBounce (try 5-6, default is 3) Check CollidesWith includes the wall's layer Increase CollisionTolerance slightly Character jitters on the ground Enable InterpolationMode.Interpolated Check that CollisionTolerance is not too small Verify the ground collider is static (not rebuilding each frame) Character cannot climb steps Increase MaxStepHeight Ensure the step geometry is clean (not sloped mesh artifacts) Check that MaxSlope is high enough that the step face is classified as a wall Character slides off slopes it should walk on Increase MaxSlope (the threshold between "ground" and "wall") Character clips through fast descending platforms The ground snapping distance may be too small for platforms moving downward faster than the snap can track. Override ComputeGroundSnappingDistance in your context to account for higher vertical platform speeds How the Collider Is Built During baking, the BaseCharacterLocomotorBaker constructs the capsule collider from your profile: Creates CapsuleGeometry from CapsuleHeight and CapsuleRadius Creates CollisionFilter from BelongsTo and CollidesWith Sets CollisionResponsePolicy.CollideRaiseCollisionEvents Hashes the geometry + filter to check if a matching blob already exists If not, creates a new CapsuleCollider blob asset Attaches it as a PhysicsCollider component Gravity The LocomotionGravity Component Gravity is stored per-entity in the LocomotionGravity component, initialized to PhysicsStep.Default.Gravity (typically (0, -9.81, 0)) during baking. The component provides two computed properties: GravityDirection - Normalized direction vector (usually (0, -1, 0)) GravityStrength - Magnitude (usually 9.81) You can modify the LocomotionGravity component at runtime to change gravity per-character. See Recipe: Per-Character Gravity. How Gravity Affects the Pipeline Gravity is not just a force applied during integration - it defines the character's entire reference frame. The GravityDirection determines what "up", "horizontal", and "vertical" mean for every step of the locomotion pipeline: Character orientation - At the start of each frame, the locomotion job reorients the character's rotation so that "up" is opposite the gravity direction. This happens before any state logic runs. Velocity decomposition - The character's velocity is split into HorizontalVelocity (perpendicular to gravity) and VerticalVelocity (along gravity). All state logic works with these decomposed values, not raw world-space velocity. Contact classification - Surfaces are classified as Ground, Wall, or Ceiling based on the angle between their normal and the gravity direction: Ground: normal-to-gravity angle below MaxSlope Wall: angle above MaxSlope but not facing away from gravity Ceiling: normal points in the same general direction as gravity Displacement correction - The Move() method projects displacement along surfaces relative to gravity. Ground contact cancels vertical displacement; wall contact projects horizontal displacement along the wall plane defined relative to gravity. Capsule orientation - All physics casts (collide-and-slide, snap-to-ground, step detection) position the capsule along the gravity axis, not world up. Snap-to-ground - The downward capsule cast is performed along GravityDirection, not (0, -1, 0). Platform inheritance - Platform velocity is split into horizontal and vertical components relative to the contact surface normal. Input and Gravity Movement input should be projected onto the plane perpendicular to gravity. The sample's Moving state (via HorizontalLocomotionBehavior) demonstrates this: float3 forwardOnPlane = movementDirection - math.projectsafe(movementDirection, -baseContext.GravityDirection); forwardOnPlane = math.normalizesafe(forwardOnPlane); This ensures "forward" always means "forward along the ground" regardless of gravity direction. Using Gravity in State Logic Your state's OnIntegrateState reads gravity from the context to compute vertical acceleration: float3 gravityAcceleration = baseContext.GravityDirection * baseContext.GravityStrength; baseContext.UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements(moveAcceleration, gravityAcceleration); Jump force is applied opposite to gravity: baseContext.VerticalVelocity = jumpForce * -baseContext.GravityDirection; Because the entire pipeline is gravity-relative, changing LocomotionGravity at runtime automatically adapts contact classification, displacement projection, capsule orientation, and ground snapping - no state logic changes needed. Next Steps Writing Custom States - Using physics data in state logic Moving Platforms - Platform velocity inheritance Troubleshooting - Common physics-related issues Recipe: Customize Ground Snapping - Advanced ground snap configuration Recipe: Per-Character Gravity - Gravity wells and custom gravity zones

manual/quickstart.html.title: Quickstart | MGM Character Controller
manual/quickstart.html.summary: Quickstart This guide gets you to a running character as fast as possible using the included sample. Goal: A capsule character that walks, jumps, and rides moving platforms. Time: Under 5 minutes. Prerequisites MGM Character Controller installed (Installation) An empty or existing Unity project with DOTS packages Step 1: Import the Sample Open Window > Package Manager Select MGM Character Controller in the package list Expand the Samples section Click Import next to Single Player Sample The sample is imported into Assets/Samples/MGM Character Controller/0.8.0/Single Player Sample/. Tip The sample ships with a ready-to-play scene (Scenes/SinglePlayerSample.unity). You can open it and press Play immediately. The steps below build a scene from scratch so you see how the pieces are wired. Step 2: Create a Scene Create a new scene (File > New Scene > Basic (Built-in)) Save it anywhere in your project Step 3: Set Up the Sub-Scene Right-click in the Hierarchy and select New Sub Scene > Empty Scene Inside the sub-scene, create a floor: 3D Object > Plane Scale the plane to (10, 1, 10) so there is room to move Add a collider to the plane Step 4: Add the Character Inside the sub-scene, create an empty GameObject named Character Add the Simple Character Character Locomotor Authoring component (search for "SimpleCharacterCharacterLocomotor" in Add Component) Assign the SimpleCharacter Profile asset from the imported sample (Assets/Samples/.../Single Player Sample/Assets/SimpleCharacter Profile) The physics profile defaults are fine for now (2m tall capsule, 0.5m radius) Step 5: Add the Player Inside the sub-scene, create another empty GameObject named Player Add the Simple Character Player Character Authoring component (search for "SimpleCharacterPlayerCharacter" in Add Component) Set the Controlled Character field to reference the Character GameObject from Step 4 Assign the SimpleCharacter Input asset from the imported sample Assign the Player (GO) prefab from the imported sample's Prefabs/ folder as the Player GO Prefab Step 6: Press Play Press Play. You should see: A capsule character standing on the plane WASD / left stick moves the character Space / gamepad south button makes the character jump The camera follows the character If Something Went Wrong Problem Fix Character falls through the floor Make sure the plane has a collider component Character doesn't move Check that the SimpleCharacter Input asset is assigned on the Player and that Unity's Input System package is installed No camera Check that the Player (GO) prefab is assigned on the Player entity Console errors about missing components Make sure you are using Unity 6000.3+ and all DOTS packages are installed What Just Happened? Three entities were created during baking: Locomotor - The character entity running in pure ECS. A Burst-compiled job processes it each fixed update through a 7-step pipeline: overlap resolution, impulse handling, integration (your state logic), collide-and-slide, ground snapping, platform inheritance, and transition evaluation. Player - Owns the input asset and camera. The PlayerGOManagerSystem instantiated the player prefab (camera + input) at runtime. Model - Follows the Locomotor via CharacterFollower and syncs its transform to a GameObject for rendering. The sample defines five states - Idling, Moving, Jumping, Falling, and Sliding - that cover basic character locomotion. Transitions between states are declared as small structs with [LocomotionTransition] attributes. Next Steps Getting Started - Create your own character from scratch with the scaffolding tool Architecture Overview - Understand the entity types and data flow Writing Custom States - Add new movement behaviors Samples - Study order for the sample code

manual/recipes/add-a-new-state.html.title: Recipe: Add a New State | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/add-a-new-state.html.summary: Recipe: Add a New State Add a new movement behavior (e.g., Dashing) to an existing state machine. When to Use You want a new movement mode that is distinct from existing states (different physics, different input handling, different transitions). Prerequisites An existing state machine created with the scaffolding tool or manually Familiarity with Writing Custom States Steps 1. Generate the state file Right-click in the Project window Select Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller > State Name it (e.g., Dashing) Press Enter This creates a new file DashingState.cs and adds the enum entry with the [LocomotionState] attribute. 2. Add profile data (if needed) If the new state needs tunable parameters, add a sub-profile: [Serializable] public struct DashProfile { public float DashSpeed; public float DashDuration; public float DashCooldown; } Add it to your main profile struct: public partial struct MyProfile : ILocomotionProfile { public MovingProfile Moving; public FallingProfile Falling; public JumpingProfile Jumping; public DashProfile Dash; // New } Update your LocomotionProfileAsset.BuildBlobAsset to copy the new fields. 3. Add state data (if needed) If the state needs to track data across frames (timers, counters), add fields to your state data struct: public partial struct MyStateData : IComponentData { public JumpData JumpData; public float DashTimer; // New public float DashCooldown; // New } 4. Implement the state logic [LocomotionState(typeof(MyStateMachine))] internal partial struct DashingState { public void OnEnterState(ref MyContext ctx) { // Set initial dash velocity in the current facing direction ctx.BaseContext.HorizontalVelocity = math.forward(ctx.BaseContext.CharacterPosition.Rotation) * ctx.Profile.Dash.DashSpeed; ctx.BaseContext.VerticalVelocity = float3.zero; ctx.StateData.DashTimer = ctx.Profile.Dash.DashDuration; } public void OnIntegrateState(ref MyContext ctx) { ref BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ref ctx.BaseContext; // Maintain dash velocity, no acceleration baseContext.UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements(); ctx.StateData.DashTimer -= baseContext.TimeStep; } public void OnExitState(ref MyContext ctx) { ctx.StateData.DashCooldown = ctx.Profile.Dash.DashCooldown; } } 5. Add transitions Create transition structs to enter and exit the new state: [LocomotionTransition(typeof(MovingState), typeof(DashingState))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(MovingToJumping))] // Higher priority than jump public struct MovingToDashing : IMyTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref MyContext ctx) => ctx.Input.DashTrigger > 0 && ctx.StateData.DashCooldown <= 0; } [LocomotionTransition(typeof(DashingState), typeof(MovingState))] public struct DashingToMoving : IMyTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref MyContext ctx) => ctx.StateData.DashTimer <= 0; } [LocomotionTransition(typeof(DashingState), typeof(FallingState))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(DashingToMoving))] public struct DashingToFalling : IMyTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref MyContext ctx) => !ctx.BaseContext.IsInContact; } 6. Add input (if needed) If the state requires a new input action (e.g., dash trigger), add it to your input struct and PlayerInputAsset. See Input System. Expected Result The character dashes forward at high speed when the dash trigger is pressed, maintains that velocity for the configured duration, then transitions back to moving (or falling if airborne). Common Mistakes Using managed types (strings, classes, arrays) in state logic - states run inside Burst-compiled jobs Not consuming trigger inputs (dash fires every frame) Related Writing Custom States - Full lifecycle reference Recipe: Add a New Transition

manual/recipes/add-a-new-transition.html.title: Recipe: Add a New Transition | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/add-a-new-transition.html.summary: Recipe: Add a New Transition Add a transition between two existing states using the [LocomotionTransition] attribute pattern. When to Use You have two states and need to define when and how the character moves from one to the other. Prerequisites Both states exist in your state machine Familiarity with Writing Custom States Steps 1. Create the transition struct Right-click in the Project window Select Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller > Transition Name it (e.g., MovingToSliding) Press Enter This creates a new file with the [LocomotionTransition] attribute. Update the generated struct to implement the generated I{Prefix}Transition interface and add your condition: [LocomotionTransition(typeof(MovingState), typeof(SlidingState))] public struct MovingToSliding : IMyTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref MyContext ctx) => ctx.BaseContext.IsSlopeAboveMax && !ctx.BaseContext.IsCeiling; } Key points: [LocomotionTransition(typeof(FromState), typeof(ToState))] tells the source generator to discover this transition and declares the source and target states ShouldTransition returns true when the transition should fire The source generator handles calling OnExitState on the source and OnEnterState on the target 2. Set priority with ordering attributes If multiple transitions can fire from the same source state, control which evaluates first: [LocomotionTransition(typeof(MovingState), typeof(JumpingState))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(MovingToIdle))] // This fires before idle check [EvaluateBefore(typeof(MovingToSliding))] // And before sliding check public struct MovingToJumping : IMyTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref MyContext ctx) => ctx.Input.JumpTrigger > 0; } The first transition that returns true wins. Higher-priority transitions should have [EvaluateBefore] pointing to lower-priority ones. See Transition Ordering for the full ordering model. 3. Compile and test Enter Play mode and trigger the conditions for your transition. Use the Entity Inspector to watch the state machine component's CurrentState value change. Expected Result When the conditions in ShouldTransition are met, the character exits the source state (OnExitState is called) and enters the target state (OnEnterState is called) at the end of the current frame. Common Mistakes Forgetting [LocomotionTransition] - the source generator will not discover the transition Circular priorities - do not create A [EvaluateBefore] B and B [EvaluateBefore] A Overly broad conditions - a transition that fires too easily can prevent other states from being reached Related Recipe: Add a New State Architecture Overview - How transitions fit into the execution loop

manual/recipes/customize-collision-respo.title: Recipe: Customize Collision Response | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/customize-collision-respo.summary: Recipe: Customize Collision Response Add custom behavior when the character hits surfaces - trampolines, breakable walls, damage zones. When to Use You want a state to react to specific surfaces during the collide-and-slide loop without replacing the default collision resolution. Prerequisites A working state machine Familiarity with The Execution Loop (Step 4: Collide-and-Slide) Steps 1. Override OnCollision on the target state OnCollision is called after each collision iteration when a new contact is detected (the contact changed during Move() and the result is not None). It does not replace the default collide-and-slide behavior — it runs after it. public void OnCollision(ref MyContext ctx) { ref readonly var contact = ref ctx.BaseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO; // Bounce only on trampoline layer (compare Unity layer index, not a bitmask) if (contact.Layer != trampolineLayer) return; if (contact.ContactType == ContactType.Ground) { BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ctx.BaseContext; baseContext.VerticalVelocity = -baseContext.VerticalVelocity * 1.5f; ctx.BaseContext = baseContext; } } 2. Use contact data for decisions When OnCollision is called, the context contains the updated contact information from the latest Move(): Property Type Description IsInContact bool Any surface contact IsGroundingContact bool Walkable ground (slope below MaxSlope) IsWall bool Surface above MaxSlope IsCeiling bool Surface above the character LocomotionContact.ValueRO.Entity Entity The contacted entity LocomotionContact.ValueRO.Normal float3 Surface normal at contact point LocomotionContact.ValueRO.BodyType BodyType Static, Kinematic, Dynamic, or Character LocomotionContact.ValueRO.Layer int Unity physics layer index of the contacted body (-1 if unfiltered) 3. Full override with OnResolveStateCollisions If you need to replace the entire collision resolution step (including Move()), override OnResolveStateCollisions instead. Both hooks are independent — overriding one does not affect the other: public void OnResolveStateCollisions(ref MyContext ctx) { BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ctx.BaseContext; // Custom collision resolution logic baseContext.Move(); ctx.BaseContext = baseContext; } Note OnResolveStateCollisions is called up to MaxBounce times per frame (once per bounce iteration). OnCollision is only called when a new contact is detected during a bounce. Expected Result The character reacts to specific surfaces with custom physics behavior (bouncing, sliding, stopping) while the standard collide-and-slide handles everything else. Common Mistakes Forgetting the copy-modify-writeback pattern when modifying ctx.BaseContext — changes are lost because BaseContext is a value type Using OnResolveStateCollisions when OnCollision would suffice — the full override is harder to maintain and requires calling Move() yourself Related The Execution Loop - Step 4: Collide-and-Slide Recipe: Push Dynamic Objects

manual/recipes/customize-ground-snapping.title: Recipe: Customize Ground Snapping | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/customize-ground-snapping.summary: Recipe: Customize Ground Snapping Override the ground snapping distance to handle slopes, speed, or state-specific behavior. When to Use Characters detach from the ground when walking down slopes or stairs at speed Characters clip through fast-moving descending platforms Prerequisites A working state machine Familiarity with The Execution Loop (Step 5: SnapToGround) How It Works The ILocomotionContext interface provides a default implementation of ComputeGroundSnappingDistance that accounts for step height, slope angle, current slope, and platform velocity. Most projects do not need to override it. If you need custom behavior, implement ComputeGroundSnappingDistance directly on your context struct — the struct method takes precedence over the default interface method: public partial struct MyContext { public void ComputeGroundSnappingDistance( in MyProfile profile, out float distance) { // Custom calculation float stepDistance = CharacterPhysicsProfile.MaxStepHeight; float slopeDistance = math.length(BaseContext.HorizontalVelocity * BaseContext.TimeStep) * math.tan(math.radians(CharacterPhysicsProfile.MaxSlope)); float platformDistance = math.length(BaseContext.PlatformVerticalVelocity) * BaseContext.TimeStep; distance = math.max(stepDistance, slopeDistance) + platformDistance; } } Note The engine already skips ground snapping when the character is moving upward (e.g., during a jump ascent). You do not need to handle that case in your override. Also note that snapping engages only when the character's vertical velocity is exactly zero; this is a documented known behavior in the behavior specification shipped with the package (Documentation~/spec/). Expected Result Characters stay grounded when walking down slopes and stairs. Characters on descending platforms do not detach. Common Mistakes Setting the snap distance too high - the character "vacuums" to the ground from unreasonable heights Forgetting platform velocity - characters lose contact with fast descending platforms Related The Execution Loop - Step 5: SnapToGround Physics Configuration - MaxStepHeight and MaxSlope Moving Platforms - Platform velocity inheritance

manual/recipes/override-pipeline-step.ht.title: Recipe: Override a Pipeline Step | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/override-pipeline-step.ht.summary: Recipe: Override a Pipeline Step Replace or wrap a step in the execution loop by overriding a DIM on your state machine struct. When to Use You need custom behavior at the pipeline level - for example, skipping integration when the character is crushed, adding pre/post logic around a step, or replacing ground snapping entirely. Prerequisites A working state machine Familiarity with The Execution Loop and Extending the Package Steps 1. Add a partial struct declaration for your state machine The source generator produces a partial struct for your state machine. Add your own partial file: // File: MyStateMachineExtensions.cs using WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Runtime.StateMachine; namespace MyGame.Locomotion { public partial struct MyStateMachine { // Override goes here } } 2. Override the pipeline method Each execution step is a DIM on ILocomotionStateMachine. Override it by defining the method on your partial struct: Example: Skip integration when crushed public partial struct MyStateMachine { public void Integrate(ref MyStateMachine stateMachine, ref MyContext context) { if (context.BaseContext.OverlapState == OverlapState.Crush) return; // Do nothing when crushed // Otherwise run the default per-state integration stateMachine.IntegratePerState(ref context); } } Example: Skip ground snap above a height threshold public partial struct MyStateMachine { public void SnapToGround(ref MyStateMachine stateMachine, ref MyContext context) { // Skip ground snap when character is above a certain height if (context.BaseContext.CharacterPosition.Position.y > 0) return; } } 3. Available overridable methods Method Calls by default Execute Full pipeline (all steps in order) HandleExternalImpulses Accumulates velocity impulses Integrate IntegratePerState SolveOverlaps Multi-plane de-collision CollideAndSlide ResolveCollisionPerState loop SnapToGround Downward capsule cast InheritDisplacementFromMotionVelocity Platform velocity inheritance EvaluateTransition EvaluateTransitionPerState See Extending the Package for the full reference. Expected Result Your custom logic runs at the correct point in the pipeline, wrapping or replacing the default behavior. Common Mistakes Forgetting to call the default implementation when you only want to add pre/post logic - the step is skipped entirely Overriding IntegratePerState or EvaluateTransitionPerState directly - these are generated dispatchers and not intended to be overridden Related Extending the Package - Full DIM customization reference The Execution Loop - What each step does

manual/recipes/per-character-gravity.htm.title: Recipe: Set Up Per-Character Gravity | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/per-character-gravity.htm.summary: Recipe: Set Up Per-Character Gravity Modify gravity per entity for gravity wells, low-gravity zones, or space sections. When to Use You want different characters to experience different gravity - for example, inside a gravity well or on a different planet. Prerequisites A working state machine Familiarity with Physics Configuration Steps 1. Write a system that modifies LocomotionGravity Gravity is stored per-entity in the LocomotionGravity component. Write a system that modifies it: [BurstCompile] [UpdateInGroup(typeof(FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup))] [UpdateBefore(typeof(MyLocomotionSystem))] partial struct GravityZoneSystem : ISystem { [BurstCompile] public void OnUpdate(ref SystemState state) { foreach (var (gravity, transform) in SystemAPI.Query<RefRW<LocomotionGravity>, RefRO<LocalTransform>>()) { float3 pos = transform.ValueRO.Position; // Example: reduce gravity in a zone if (IsInLowGravityZone(pos)) { gravity.ValueRW.Gravity = new float3(0, -4.9f, 0); // Half gravity } else { gravity.ValueRW.Gravity = new float3(0, -9.81f, 0); // Normal } } } } 2. Schedule before the locomotion system Use [UpdateBefore(typeof(MyLocomotionSystem))] so the gravity is set before the locomotion job reads it. 3. Gravity direction changes For non-downward gravity (e.g., walking on walls or ceilings), set the gravity direction: gravity.ValueRW.Gravity = new float3(1, 0, 0) * 9.81f; // Gravity pulls to the right The BaseLocomotionContext decomposes this into GravityDirection and GravityStrength, which your state logic uses for integration. Expected Result Characters in the gravity zone fall slower (or in a different direction). The state machine and collide-and-slide algorithm adapt automatically because they read GravityDirection and GravityStrength from the context. Common Mistakes Scheduling after the locomotion system - the old gravity value is used for the current frame Modifying GravityDirection directly on the context inside a state - this is overwritten each frame from the component. Modify the LocomotionGravity component instead. Related Physics Configuration - LocomotionGravity section Moving Platforms - Gravity wells in the sample

manual/recipes/push-dynamic-objects.html.title: Recipe: Push Dynamic Objects on Collision | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/push-dynamic-objects.html.summary: Recipe: Push Dynamic Objects on Collision Apply velocity impulses to dynamic rigid bodies when the character collides with them. The baseline behavior — push impulses scaling with the character's mass — is specified as DYN-1 in the behavior specification shipped with the package (Documentation~/spec/). When to Use You want the character to push crates, barrels, or other dynamic physics objects when walking into them. Prerequisites A working state machine Dynamic rigid bodies in your scene with PhysicsBody (set to Dynamic) Steps 1. Override OnCollision In the states where you want push behavior (typically MovingState), add push logic in OnCollision: public void OnCollision(ref MyContext ctx) { ref readonly var contact = ref ctx.BaseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO; if (contact.BodyType != BodyType.Dynamic) return; BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ctx.BaseContext; float3 pushVelocity = math.normalizesafe(baseContext.HorizontalVelocity) * math.length(baseContext.HorizontalVelocity) * 0.5f; // Apply impulse to the dynamic body baseContext.ApplyImpulse( ref baseContext, contact.BodyIndex, contact.Entity, baseContext.PhysicsWorld.GetRigidBodyIndex(baseContext.CharacterEntity), baseContext.CharacterEntity, pushVelocity); ctx.BaseContext = baseContext; } OnCollision is called when a new contact is detected, which means the impulse is applied once per contact — not every bounce iteration. 2. Tune the push force Adjust the multiplier (0.5f above) based on your game's feel. Higher values push objects further. The character's Mass and MassToDynamic on the physics profile also affect the default impulse behavior from HandleExternalImpulses. Expected Result When the character walks into a dynamic body, the body is pushed in the direction the character is moving. The push force scales with the character's speed. Common Mistakes Using the copy-modify-writeback pattern but forgetting ctx.BaseContext = baseContext at the end - the impulse is lost Applying impulse in OnIntegrateState instead of a collision hook - contacts are not available yet during integration Related The Execution Loop - Step 4: Collide-and-Slide Physics Configuration - Mass and MassToDynamic Recipe: Customize Collision Response

manual/recipes/run-multiple-state-machin.title: Recipe: Run Multiple State Machines | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/run-multiple-state-machin.summary: Recipe: Run Multiple State Machines Use different state machine types for different character archetypes in the same project. When to Use Your game has fundamentally different movement types - for example, ground characters and vehicles - that should not share a state enum. Prerequisites One working state machine already created Familiarity with Creating a State Machine Steps 1. Create a second state machine Use the scaffolding tool again: Right-click in a different folder in the Project window Select Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller > StateMachine Name it (e.g., Vehicle) This generates a completely independent set of types: VehicleStateMachine, VehicleStates, VehicleContext, VehicleProfile, VehicleInput, VehicleStateData, and all authoring/editor files. 2. Define states and transitions for the new machine Each state machine has its own enum, states, transitions, profile, and input. They are fully independent - no shared types needed. 3. Create entities with the new machine Use the generated VehicleCharacterLocomotorAuthoring and VehiclePlayerCharacterAuthoring components on new entities. Each state machine type generates its own authoring components and systems. 4. Both run simultaneously The source generator creates a separate ISystem for each state machine type. Both systems schedule their own LocomotionJob independently, processing their respective entities in parallel. Expected Result Ground characters and vehicles coexist in the same scene, each with their own state machine, states, transitions, and physics behavior. They share the same BaseLocomotionContext and collide-and-slide infrastructure. Switching an entity between state machines This is an advanced pattern. To switch a character from one state machine to another (e.g., entering a vehicle), you need to: Remove the components of the old state machine (state machine, input, profile, state data) Add the components of the new state machine This involves structural entity changes, which should happen via an EntityCommandBuffer. Common Mistakes Trying to share states between state machines - states are bound to a specific state machine via [LocomotionState(typeof(...))] Putting both state machine's components on the same entity - each entity should have exactly one state machine type Related Creating a State Machine - Scaffolding tool Extending the Package - Architecture details

manual/recipes/setup-hybrid-character.ht.title: Recipe: Set Up a Hybrid Character | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/setup-hybrid-character.ht.summary: Recipe: Set Up a Hybrid Character Create a character with both ECS locomotion and a visual GameObject model. When to Use You want a character driven by the Burst-compiled locomotion job that also has a visible 3D model with an Animator, particle effects, audio, or other MonoBehaviour-based features. Prerequisites A working state machine created with the scaffolding tool or manually Familiarity with Hybrid GameObject Layer concepts Steps 1. Create the Locomotor entity (in sub-scene) Add your Character Locomotor Authoring component as described in Getting Started. 2. Create the Model (in sub-scene) Add a child GameObject under (or near) the Locomotor with your visual mesh/model Add a CharacterFollowerAuthoring component Set the Locomotor field to reference the Locomotor's authoring component The model can have an Animator, AudioSource, particle systems, etc. 3. Create the Player prefab (regular GameObject, NOT in sub-scene) Create a GameObject with Camera, CinemachineBrain, PlayerInput Add a PlayerGoAuthoring component with camera references Save it as a prefab 4. Create the Player entity (in sub-scene) Create a GameObject in the sub-scene Add your Player Character Authoring component Assign the character entity, input asset, and player GO prefab What Happens at Runtime The Player entity is baked, triggering PlayerGoManagerSystem to instantiate the player prefab The input asset is initialized with the player's camera and input references The model entity follows the Locomotor via CharacterFollowerSystem The model's GameObject transform is synced via EntityGoTransformSyncSystem Next Steps Integration: Animation - Connecting an Animator to a hybrid character Integration: Cinemachine - Camera setup on player GameObjects

manual/recipes/setup-moving-platform.htm.title: Recipe: Set Up a Moving Platform | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/setup-moving-platform.htm.summary: Recipe: Set Up a Moving Platform Create a moving or rotating platform that characters can ride. When to Use You want a kinematic body that moves along a track or rotates, and characters standing on it should automatically inherit its velocity and rotation. Prerequisites A sub-scene with physics enabled Familiarity with Moving Platforms concepts Steps 1. Create the platform GameObject (in sub-scene) Create a GameObject with your platform mesh Add a physics collider (Box, Mesh, etc.) Set the collider as Kinematic (not Dynamic, not Static) 2. Add platform authoring Add a PlatformAuthoring component. 3. Add movement behavior Add a MovingPlatformAuthoring component and configure: Speed: Movement speed along the track in world units per second Rotation: Rotation axis and speed (float3) Track (optional): Define waypoints for the platform to follow 4. Collision layers Ensure the platform's collision layer is included in your character's CollidesWith mask. By default, both use all layers, so this works out of the box. Next Steps Moving Platforms - How platform inheritance works Physics Configuration - Collision layer setup

manual/recipes/switch-to-ai-input.html.title: Recipe: Switch a Character to AI Input | MGM Character Controller
manual/recipes/switch-to-ai-input.html.summary: Recipe: Switch a Character to AI Input Drive a character with an AI system instead of player input. When to Use You want NPC characters that use the same state machine and movement logic as players, but are controlled by AI decision-making instead of hardware input. Prerequisites A working character with a state machine Familiarity with Input System Steps 1. Create a tag component public struct AIControlled : IComponentData { } Add this to AI-controlled character entities during baking (via an authoring component or a system). 2. Create an AI input system Write a system that writes directly to the input ECS component, bypassing PlayerInputAsset: [BurstCompile] [UpdateInGroup(typeof(SimulationSystemGroup))] partial struct AIInputSystem : ISystem { [BurstCompile] public void OnUpdate(ref SystemState state) { foreach (var (input, transform) in SystemAPI.Query<RefRW<MyInput>, RefRO<LocalTransform>>() .WithAll<AIControlled>()) { // Example: move toward a target position float3 targetDir = math.normalizesafe( GetTargetPosition() - transform.ValueRO.Position); input.ValueRW.Movement = targetDir; input.ValueRW.JumpTrigger = ShouldJump() ? 1f : 0f; } } } 3. Skip the Player entity for AI characters AI characters do not need a Player entity, player prefab, or PlayerInputAsset. They only need the Locomotor entity with the state machine components and the AIControlled tag. During baking, add the input component directly without the player input pipeline: public class AICharacterAuthoring : MonoBehaviour { // Baking adds MyInput component + AIControlled tag } 4. (Optional) Shared state machine The AI character uses the exact same state machine, states, transitions, profile, and physics as player characters. No code changes needed in the state machine - it only reads the TInput component, which is written by your AI system instead of the player input pipeline. Expected Result AI characters move, jump, and transition between states identically to player characters. The only difference is the source of input data. Common Mistakes Forgetting to add the input component to the AI entity - the locomotion system will not process it Writing input every frame without accumulating triggers - jump triggers can be missed between fixed updates (use the same accumulation pattern as player input) Related Input System - Full input architecture Architecture Overview - Entity types and roles

manual/samples.html.title: Samples | MGM Character Controller
manual/samples.html.summary: Samples This page lists all samples included with the MGM Character Controller and provides a recommended study order. SinglePlayerSample Teaches Complete state machine with five states, transitions, input handling, camera setup, and profile configuration Difficulty Beginner to intermediate Setup time 5 minutes (see Quickstart) Dependencies Unity Input System, Cinemachine What It Contains The sample provides a full reference implementation of a third-person character controller: 5 states: Idling, Moving, Jumping, Falling, Sliding 17 transitions: All valid state-to-state transitions with priority ordering 3 behavior structs: Reusable gravity, horizontal locomotion, and jump-arc logic shared across states Input handling: Camera-relative movement with jump trigger accumulation Profile: Tunable walk/run speed, acceleration, jump arcs, gravity, and terminal velocity Prefabs: Character (Locomotor + Model) and Player (Camera + Input) Assets: Pre-configured profile and input ScriptableObjects Scene: A ready-to-play playground (Scenes/SinglePlayerSample.unity) with stairs, slopes, conveyors, elevators, bridges, and rotating platforms Key Files - Study Order Read the sample code in this order to build the mental model (all paths relative to Scripts/SimpleCharacter/): Order File What It Teaches 1 Runtime/SimpleCharacterStateMachine.cs The anchor struct - [LocomotionStateMachine] attribute triggers source generation 2 Runtime/Data/SimpleCharacterInput.cs Input struct with continuous (Movement, IsSprinting, IsJumping) and trigger (JumpTrigger) fields, plus accumulation in ApplyInputsToCharacter 3 Runtime/Data/SimpleCharacterProfile.cs Profile struct composed of per-state sub-profiles (Moving.Profile, Falling.Profile, Jumping.Profile) plus AirControlFactor 4 Runtime/Data/SimpleCharacterStateData.cs Per-state persistent data (JumpData with jump count and apex timer) 5 Runtime/States/Idling.cs Simplest state - zeros velocity on enter, empty integrate 6 Runtime/States/Moving.cs Walk/run speed selection and horizontal acceleration via HorizontalLocomotionBehavior 7 Runtime/States/Falling.cs Gravity with terminal velocity via GravityBehavior; rotates to face input with no horizontal acceleration 8 Runtime/States/Jumping.cs Air control (HorizontalLocomotionBehavior scaled by AirControlFactor) + jump arc via JumpBehavior 9 Runtime/States/Sliding.cs Gravity-driven sliding on steep slopes, reusing GravityBehavior 10 Runtime/States/Behaviors/ GravityBehavior, HorizontalLocomotionBehavior, JumpBehavior - reusable behavior structs states compose 11 Runtime/States/Transitions/ 17 transitions split across From*.cs / To*.cs files, with [LocomotionTransition] and [EvaluateBefore] for priority ordering 12 Runtime/ReorientGravityToContactSurface.cs + Runtime/System/ReorientGravityToContactSurfaceSystem.cs Opt-in gravity reorientation to the contact surface (wall-walking / gravity pads) 13 Authoring/SimpleCharacterPlayerInputAsset.cs Camera-relative input reading from the Player GO prefab's camera 14 Authoring/SimpleCharacterProfileAsset.cs Designer-facing jump parameters converted to runtime physics values at bake time Things to Try After running the sample, try these modifications to deepen your understanding: Change movement speed - Open the SimpleCharacter Profile asset and modify Moving > WalkSpeed / RunSpeed. Notice how the profile is baked, so you need to re-enter Play mode. Enable double jump - In the profile asset, add a second entry to the Jumps list. JumpBehavior already supports chained jumps via StateData.JumpData.JumpsCount. Disable air control - In the profile asset, set AirControlFactor to 0. The character will maintain its launch velocity with no air steering. Add debug visualization - Select the character entity in the sub-scene and add a LocomotionDebugConfigAuthoring component. Enter Play mode and observe contact points and movement paths in the Scene view. Related Docs Quickstart - Set up and run this sample Writing Custom States - How the state lifecycle works Creating a State Machine - How the scaffolding tool generates this structure Input System - Input architecture in depth FlyCamSample Teaches Minimal single-state fly camera, gravity-free movement, split entity/camera rotation, collision handling without ground contact Difficulty Beginner Setup time 5 minutes Dependencies Unity Input System What It Contains A first-person fly camera controller for navigating test scenes. The camera floats freely without gravity, slides along obstacles, and uses mouse look for rotation. 1 state: Flying (always active — no transitions needed) No gravity: Zero vertical acceleration, ground snapping disabled Split rotation: Entity rotates in yaw only; pitch is applied to the camera GameObject Collision: Slides along walls and ceilings via the default collide-and-slide pipeline Input: WASD/ZQSD movement, mouse look, Space to fly up, Left Ctrl to fly down Controls Input Action W / Z Move forward S Move backward A / Q Strafe left D Strafe right Mouse Look (yaw + pitch) Space Fly up Left Ctrl Fly down Movement follows the camera look direction — looking down and pressing forward moves the camera downward toward where it is looking. How It Works Architecture The FlyCam follows the same Player → Character entity split as the SinglePlayerSample but is intentionally minimal: classDiagram direction LR class PlayerEntity["Player Entity"] { CharacterFollower LocomotionInputAsset PlayerGameObjectPrefab } class CharacterEntity["Character Entity"] { FlyCamStateMachine FlyCamInput FlyCamStateData ~yaw~ FlyCamProfile LocomotionVelocity LocomotionContact PhysicsCollider ~capsule~ } class PlayerGo["PlayerGo (GameObject)"] { PlayerGoAuthoring PlayerInput } class CameraTarget["CameraTarget (Transform)"] { Camera } PlayerEntity --> CharacterEntity : CharacterFollower PlayerEntity ..> PlayerGo : instantiates at runtime PlayerGo --> CameraTarget : child transform Rotation: Entity vs Camera The entity only rotates around the gravity axis (yaw). This is necessary because the locomotion pipeline applies gravity alignment before the state runs, which would fight with any pitch applied to the entity. Pitch is handled entirely on the managed (GameObject) side: FlyCamPlayerInputAsset.ReadInputsFromAsset accumulates pitch from mouse Y delta It applies pitch as localRotation on the Camera transform It passes the pitch angle to the ECS input struct so the state can compute a pitched movement direction // In FlyCamPlayerInputAsset — managed side m_Pitch = Mathf.Clamp(m_Pitch - look.y * LookSensitivity, -MaxPitch, MaxPitch); m_CameraTransform.localRotation = Quaternion.Euler(m_Pitch, 0f, 0f); inputs.Pitch = m_Pitch; // In FlyCamFlyingState — ECS side (yaw only on entity) quaternion rotation = quaternion.AxisAngle(up, math.radians(stateData.Yaw)); baseContext.CharacterPosition.Rotation = rotation; // Pitched forward for movement direction quaternion pitchedRotation = math.mul(rotation, quaternion.AxisAngle(math.right(), math.radians(ctx.Input.Pitch))); float3 forward = math.mul(pitchedRotation, math.forward()); Movement Without Gravity The state computes desired velocity from input and uses MathematicsHelpers.ComputeAccelerationToTargetVelocity for smooth acceleration/deceleration. No gravity acceleration is applied — both horizontal and vertical channels are purely input-driven. The desired direction is split into horizontal and vertical components relative to the gravity axis, then passed to UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements with zero gravity contribution. Ground Snapping Disabled The FlyCamContext partial overrides ComputeGroundSnappingDistance to return zero, preventing the snap-to-ground step from pulling the camera to the floor: public partial struct FlyCamContext { public void ComputeGroundSnappingDistance(in FlyCamProfile profile, out float distance) { distance = 0f; } } Stale Contact Clearing A flying entity has no transitions to clear the contact state (unlike a grounded character that transitions to Falling). Without clearing, a contact from a previous collision would persist and cause Move() to project displacement incorrectly on subsequent frames. The state clears the contact at the start of each integration: baseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRW = LocomotionContact.None; The collide-and-slide step will set a fresh contact if a collision occurs that frame. Scene Setup The sample scene contains: Subscene with: A character entity (capsule collider) with FlyCamCharacterLocomotionAuthoring — assigns the profile asset and configures the physics capsule A player entity with FlyCamPlayerCharacterAuthoring — references the character, input asset, and PlayerGo prefab PlayerGo prefab (instantiated at runtime): PlayerGoAuthoring component with Camera and CameraTarget references PlayerInput component bound to FlyCamActionMap A CameraTarget child Transform with the Camera as its child Important The Camera must be a child of the CameraTarget Transform. The CameraRigFollowControlledCharacterSystem moves the CameraTarget to match the character entity's position. The Camera inherits that position and adds its own local pitch rotation. Key Files - Study Order Order File What It Teaches 1 Runtime/FlyCamStateMachine.cs Minimal state machine anchor — single [LocomotionStateMachine] attribute 2 Runtime/Data/FlyCamInput.cs Input with continuous (Movement, Pitch), accumulated (LookDelta +=), and overwritten (VerticalMovement) fields 3 Runtime/Data/FlyCamProfile.cs Simple profile with just movement tuning and look sensitivity 4 Runtime/Data/FlyCamStateData.cs Minimal state data — only yaw angle 5 Runtime/Data/FlyCamContextExtensions.cs Overriding a DIM default to disable ground snapping 6 Runtime/States/FlyCamFlyingState.cs Core logic: split yaw/pitch rotation, pitched movement direction, zero-gravity movement, stale contact clearing 7 Runtime/Data/FlyCamPlayerInputAsset.cs Managed-side pitch handling, camera rotation, Input System action reading Things to Try Adjust fly speed - Open the FlyCamProfileAsset and change Moving > MaxSpeed. Higher values make the camera faster. TimeToMaxSpeed and TimeToStop control acceleration and deceleration feel. Change mouse sensitivity - Modify LookSensitivity on either the FlyCamProfileAsset (affects yaw) or the FlyCamPlayerInputAsset (affects pitch). Disable collision - Either set the physics profile's collision filter to collide with nothing in the FlyCamCharacterLocomotionAuthoring inspector, or override OnResolveStateCollisions in FlyCamFlyingState to move the locomotor directly without any collision check. Both approaches help understand what the collide-and-slide pipeline does. Add a speed boost - Create a second profile with higher MaxSpeed and swap profiles at runtime, or add a sprint input to the action map. Related Docs Creating a State Machine - Full scaffolding walkthrough Writing Custom States - State lifecycle and DIM overrides Input System - Player → Character input pipeline Customize Ground Snapping - More on the ComputeGroundSnappingDistance override Customize Collision Response - Overriding OnResolveStateCollisions BehaviorShowCase Teaches The controller's behavior envelope — one focused subscene per behavior, loadable at runtime, plus stress-testing tools Difficulty Intermediate Setup time 2 minutes (open Scenes/BehaviourTests.unity and press Play) Dependencies Unity Input System What It Contains A behavior gallery built around the SimpleCharacter state machine from the SinglePlayerSample. The main scene (Scenes/BehaviourTests.unity) hosts a runtime scene-picker UI; each entry streams in one small subscene that demonstrates a single behavior with a bot-driven character, so you can study or regression-check behaviors in isolation. 28 behavior subscenes, organized by category under Scenes/BehaviourTests/: Category Subscenes What They Cover Locomotion 4 Slope grounding, jumping on flat ground, jumping through one-way platforms, stair step-up CharacterCollision 3 Head-on character collisions, stacked characters, overlap depenetration DynamicBody 7 Pushing light/medium/heavy spheres, sphere-drop impacts at various masses and heights DynamicBridge 3 Walking across a dynamic bridge, character and dynamic-body impacts on it KinematicPlatform 7 Elevator, conveyor, spinner, one-way platform grounding; crusher, pusher, rotating-bat collisions Balance 4 Edge balancing: character vs character and character vs dynamic body, in both directions Runtime tools (under Runtime/ and Bot/): TestSceneSelector - UI Toolkit scene picker driven by a TestSceneCatalog asset: hover a category, click an entry to load/unload its subscene. Includes a timestep slider that changes the fixed update rate (Hz) live by writing the FixedStepRate singleton and the FixedStepSimulationSystemGroup timestep (see Fixed Step Rate). Bot input (SimpleCharacterBotAuthoring + SimpleCharacterBotBakingSystem) - bakes a constant Move direction and a one-shot JumpTrigger directly into the character's SimpleCharacterInput, so each subscene's character acts without a player or a runtime input system. SpawningSystem + TestSpawner / SpawnConfig - input-driven stress spawning in seven patterns (sphere, grid, cube, circle, line, random scatter, single-at-click). Tab cycles the pattern, Enter batch-spawns, Shift+LMB spawns one, Backspace clears. GravityWellAuthoring + GravityWellSystem - overrides locomotion gravity for characters within range of a gravity-well entity (per-character gravity demo). PerfTests - Scenes/PerfTests.unity with a PerfSpawner subscene for measuring the controller under large entity counts using the spawn patterns above. Things to Try Compare timesteps - Load KinematicPlatform > Grounding_Elevator and drag the timestep slider from 60 Hz down to 15 Hz to see how the behavior holds up at low tick rates. Stress-test - Open Scenes/PerfTests.unity, press Enter to spawn a batch, and watch the profiler; press Tab to switch spawn patterns. Add your own behavior scene - Copy one of the subscenes, modify the setup, and add an entry to the TestSceneCatalog asset so it appears in the picker. Related Docs Fixed Step Rate - The FixedStepRate singleton behind the timestep slider Recipe: Per-Character Gravity - The pattern behind the gravity well Recipe: Switch to AI Input - Driving characters without a player Museum Tour - The same 29 exhibits, presented hands-off Museum Tour Teaches The controller's whole behavior range in one hands-off pass, plus a runtime application of AI-driven input on streamed-in characters Difficulty Beginner to watch, intermediate to read Setup time 1 minute (open Scenes/Museum.unity and press Play) Dependencies The Behavior Showcase and Single Player samples, imported first Where the BehaviorShowCase is a Gym — you pick an exhibit and study it — the Museum is a curated presentation: it picks for you. Press Play, touch nothing, and it cycles all 29 behavior exhibits one at a time, each for exactly as long as that behavior is characterized over, with a placard naming what is on screen. Use it for a first impression, a demo reel, or a five-minute look at what the package does; use the Gym when you want to stop on one behavior. Important The Museum ships no characters, geometry, or behavior of its own — it streams the Behavior Showcase's subscenes and uses the Single Player sample's reference character. Import both samples before importing this one, or the tour has nothing to show. What It Contains Scenes/Museum.unity - the only entry point: a camera framed like the Behavior Showcase's own scene, a directional light, the shared World subscene (physics step + ground plane), and the MuseumDirector GameObject carrying the placard UIDocument. Runtime/Resources/MuseumCatalog.asset - the generated tour data: 29 rows of category, exhibit name, entity-scene reference, and dwell, in tour order. Array order is tour order. MuseumTourSequencer - the tour lifecycle as plain C#: which exhibit is current, whether it is still loading or on display, how much dwell is left, when to hand over. It owns no clock and no world (both the frame delta and "is the exhibit visible yet" are passed in), which is why the whole lifecycle is covered by EditMode tests with no scene and no Play mode. MuseumPlacard - the pure text projection behind the on-screen label: category, exhibit name, and either a whole-second countdown or Loading…. MuseumDirector - the only place the sample touches the engine: it streams the exhibit the sequencer asks for, writes the three placard labels, and creates the MuseumTour gate entity. MuseumBotCaptureSystem + MuseumBotReArmSystem - two Burst ISystems that keep the jump exhibits jumping (see Keeping the jump exhibits going). MuseumSampleBuilder (Editor) - regenerates the catalog and the scene from one 29-row table. How to Use It Import Behavior Showcase and Single Player Sample from Window > Package Manager > Samples. Import Museum Tour from the same list. Open Scenes/Museum.unity. Press Play, and do not touch anything — there is no menu, no selection step, and no input path. Expected result: within a moment the first exhibit (Locomotion / Jump - Flat Ground) streams in and the placard in the bottom-left reads its category, its name, and a countdown from 3 s. When the countdown runs out that exhibit is unloaded, the next one is loaded, and the placard reads Loading… until it is visible. After all 29 exhibits the tour wraps back to the first and keeps going indefinitely. What a common failure looks like: the tour sits on Loading… for 10 seconds and then moves to the next exhibit. That is the deliberate give-up path — an exhibit that cannot be streamed never halts the tour, and it is attempted again on the next lap. If every exhibit does this, the Behavior Showcase sample is not imported, so the scenes the catalog points at do not exist in your project. Tour Order and Dwell The order is the Gym picker's own order and wording, with Jump - Moving Platform — the one behavior subscene the picker does not list — appended to the end of its category: Order Category Exhibits Dwell range 1 Locomotion 4 3-5 s 2 Character Collision 3 5-10 s 3 Kinematic Platform 8 5-30 s 4 Dynamic Body 7 5-10 s 5 Dynamic Bridge 3 5 s 6 Balance 4 10 s Each dwell is the duration that scene is characterized over by the golden-master suite, so an exhibit is on display for exactly as long as its behavior is known to be interesting — Jump - Flat Ground for 3 s, Conveyor for 14 s, Crusher for 30 s. Jump - Moving Platform has no characterization run, so the spec mints 8 s for it. One lap is 278 s of dwell (4 min 38 s) plus loading time. The dwell clock starts when the exhibit becomes visible, not when it is selected, so streaming time is never charged against the time you get to watch it. Because each handover unloads the previous exhibit and the next lap re-loads it from its baked file, every lap replays each exhibit from its start: the dropped sphere falls again, the stacked characters collide again — you never see a lap of settled leftovers. Keeping the Jump Exhibits Going Three exhibits are jumps (Jump - Flat Ground, Jump - One-Way Platforms, Jump - Moving Platform). Their characters are bot-driven by the Behavior Showcase's baker, which bakes a one-shot jump trigger — enough for a single jump, which would leave most of a 3-8 s dwell showing a character standing still. The Museum re-arms it, and this is a runtime application of the Switch to AI Input recipe: write the input component directly from a system, and the state machine cannot tell the difference. MuseumBotCaptureSystem runs in InitializationSystemGroup after the scene-streaming group, so it snapshots each streamed-in character's pristine baked JumpTrigger before any tick can consume it. The snapshot lives on the character entity, so it dies with the exhibit and is retaken on the next lap. MuseumBotReArmSystem restores that value once the character reports a ground contact and its trigger has been consumed — one field, one condition, no accumulation. Two consequences worth knowing, because they are what keep the exhibits honest: A character with nothing baked is never written to. The snapshot carries no movement and no other intent, so the Museum structurally cannot perform an exhibit that does not jump — what you see on a push, balance, or platform exhibit is the exhibit, not a Museum performance of it. Both systems require a MuseumTour gate entity that only MuseumDirector creates, at runtime, in the Museum scene. There is no authoring component and no baker for it, so with the Museum merely imported and not playing, both systems are inert everywhere else in your project — including in the package's own characterization suites, which reproduce bitwise with the sample installed. Regenerating the Sample The catalog and the scene are generated, not hand-maintained. MuseumSampleBuilder.TourOrder is the single source of truth for the 29 rows; everything else is derived from it. Menu item What it does MGM > Museum > Rebuild Catalog Rewrites Runtime/Resources/MuseumCatalog.asset from the tour table, resolving each row to its behavior scene MGM > Museum > Rebuild Scene Rebuilds Scenes/Museum.unity (camera, light, World subscene, director + placard panel) MGM > Museum > Rebuild All Both, in that order All three overwrite in place rather than delete and recreate, so asset GUIDs — and therefore the scene's references — survive a rebuild. Rebuilding the catalog from an unchanged table is a byte-level no-op, which the test suite asserts. Things to Try Change a dwell - Edit the row's DwellSeconds in MuseumSampleBuilder.TourOrder, run MGM > Museum > Rebuild Catalog, and press Play. Watch the placard count down from the new value. (Editing the generated asset directly works too, but the next rebuild overwrites it.) Reorder the tour - Move a row in TourOrder and rebuild the catalog. Array order is tour order, so the Museum immediately follows the new order — including where the lap wraps. Watch the re-arm - Let Jump - Flat Ground play and count the jumps in its 3 s. Then open MuseumBotReArmSystem and comment out the re-arm assignment: the character now jumps once and stands still for the rest of the dwell, which is what the one-shot baked trigger does on its own. Verify the gate - Load a Behavior Showcase subscene from the Gym picker with the Museum sample installed. Nothing jumps by itself: without the Museum scene playing there is no MuseumTour entity, so neither Museum system runs.
