manual/transition-ordering.html.title: Transition Ordering | MGM Character Controller
manual/transition-ordering.html.summary: Transition Ordering When several transitions leave the same source state, the order they are evaluated in matters: the first matching transition wins. The [EvaluateBefore] and [EvaluateAfter] attributes let you declare that order explicitly, following the same pattern as Unity's [UpdateBefore] / [UpdateAfter] system ordering. Declaring Order Add the attributes to a transition struct, referencing other transition types from the same source state. Both attributes allow multiple uses: [LocomotionTransition(typeof(Moving), typeof(Jumping))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(FromMovingToIdling))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(FromMovingToFalling))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(FromMovingToSliding))] public struct FromMovingToJumping : ISimpleCharacterTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref SimpleCharacterContext ctx) => /* ... */; } Here the jump transition is checked before the idle, fall, and slide transitions - so pressing jump while running always wins. How the Order Is Resolved For each source state, the source generator collects all [LocomotionTransition] structs and topologically sorts them from the [EvaluateBefore] / [EvaluateAfter] constraints. The generated evaluation is a simple chain of ShouldTransition checks in that order - the first one that returns true fires (calling OnExitState on the source and OnEnterState on the target) and evaluation stops for the frame. Rules to be aware of: First match wins - at most one transition fires per entity per fixed update. Constraints are per source state - a constraint referencing a transition of a different source state is ignored. Unconstrained transitions keep declaration order relative to each other. Cyclic constraints fall back to declaration order - if the constraints contradict each other (A before B, B before A), the generator cannot sort them and evaluates all of that state's transitions in declaration order instead. There is no error; prefer expressing the order with the fewest constraints necessary. The ordering is resolved once at compile time by the source generator, so there is no runtime sorting cost. Next Steps Writing Custom States - The transition struct pattern in full Recipe: Add a New Transition - Step-by-step guide Best Practices - Recommended transition priorities

manual/troubleshooting.html.title: Troubleshooting | MGM Character Controller
manual/troubleshooting.html.summary: Troubleshooting This page lists common issues organized by symptom. For each issue: what you see, why it happens, and how to fix it. Character falls through the floor Cause: The floor does not have a physics collider that the ECS world can see. Fix: Select the floor GameObject inside the sub-scene Add a collider component to the floor Verify the sub-scene is loaded (check Hierarchy for the sub-scene icon) Verify: Enter Play mode. Open the Physics Debugger (Window > Analysis > Physics Debugger) and confirm the floor collider is visible. Prevention: Always ensure environment geometry inside sub-scenes has a collider. Character doesn't respond to input Cause: Input is not flowing from the hardware to the ECS component. Fix - check each layer in order: Input System package: Confirm com.unity.inputsystem is installed and the Active Input Handling is set to Input System Package (New) or Both in Edit > Project Settings > Player Player entity: Verify the Player entity has the input asset assigned in the Player Character Authoring component Player prefab: The Player GO Prefab must have a PlayerInput component with input actions assigned Character reference: The Player entity must reference the correct Character entity Verify: Add a breakpoint or log in your PlayerInputAsset.ReadInputsFromAsset() method to confirm it is called each frame. Character jitters on the ground Cause: The character's visual position updates discretely each fixed step, causing visible stuttering. Fix: Set InterpolationMode to Interpolated in the Character Physics Profile If still jittering, increase CollisionTolerance slightly (try 0.01) Verify the ground collider is static (not a dynamic body rebuilding each frame) Verify: The jitter should disappear or become imperceptible at 60+ FPS. Character walks through walls Cause: The collide-and-slide algorithm does not have enough iterations to resolve the collision. Fix: Increase MaxBounce on the Character Physics Profile (try 5-6, default is 3) Check that the wall's collision layer is included in the character's CollidesWith mask If the character is moving very fast, the displacement per frame may exceed the collider size - reduce speed or increase the fixed update rate Verify: Enable debug visualization with contact points to see if wall contacts are being detected. Character cannot climb steps Cause: Step detection conditions are not met. Fix: Increase MaxStepHeight on the Character Physics Profile Ensure MaxSlope is high enough that the step's vertical face is classified as a wall (not ground) Verify the step geometry is clean - sloped mesh artifacts can confuse the step detector Verify: Enable debug visualization. Wall contacts should appear at the step face, followed by successful upward movement. Character slides off walkable slopes Cause: The slope angle exceeds the MaxSlope threshold. Fix: Increase MaxSlope on the Character Physics Profile. The default handles most cases at 45-60 degrees. Verify: Log or inspect ctx.BaseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO.Normal to compute the actual slope angle. Jump doesn't fire Cause: The jump trigger input is being overwritten instead of accumulated, or it is not being consumed after use. Fix: In your ICharacterLocomotionInput.ApplyInputsToCharacter, accumulate the trigger: JumpTrigger += playerInputs.JumpTrigger (not JumpTrigger = playerInputs.JumpTrigger) In your PlayerInputAsset.ReadInputsFromAsset, return 1f for the trigger only on the frame the button was pressed (WasPerformedThisFrame()), not while it is held Verify: Add a temporary log in ApplyInputsToCharacter to see the accumulated value. Jump fires every frame Cause: The jump trigger is not being consumed (reset to zero) after use. Fix: After reading the trigger value in your state's OnIntegrateState, reset it: LocomotionInput value = ctx.Input; value.JumpTrigger = 0; ctx.Input = value; Verify: The character should jump once per button press, not continuously. State transition never fires Cause: The transition's conditions are not met, or a higher-priority transition is firing first. Fix: Check the [EvaluateBefore] attributes on your transitions - they control evaluation order. The first matching transition wins. Verify the conditions in your ShouldTransition method match the actual runtime state. Use the Entity Inspector to check LocomotionContact, LocomotionVelocity, and your input component values. Confirm the transition struct has a [LocomotionTransition(typeof(FromState), typeof(ToState))] attribute pointing at the right source state - a transition declared for another source state is never evaluated while this state is active. Verify: Add a temporary log inside the transition's ShouldTransition to see which condition fails. Character launched unexpectedly Cause: An external impulse is applied from a dynamic body collision, or platform velocity is being applied twice. Fix: Enable impulse debug visualization to see where forces are coming from Check that you are not manually adding PlatformHorizontalVelocity in OnIntegrateState - the system handles platform inheritance automatically in the ComputeInheritedDisplacement step If dynamic body collisions are injecting too much velocity, check the Mass and MassToDynamic values on the Character Physics Profile Verify: Disable impulse handling temporarily by overriding HandleExternalImpulses to a no-op on your state machine struct. Character clips through or gets stuck on moving platforms Cause: The ground snapping distance is too small for the platform's speed. Fix: The default ComputeGroundSnappingDistance on ILocomotionContext already accounts for platform vertical velocity. If you have overridden it on your context struct, ensure your implementation includes platform velocity in the distance calculation. See Recipe: Customize Ground Snapping for details. Verify: Enable path point debug visualization to see if the character loses ground contact on fast platforms. Source generator not producing code Cause: The source generator cannot find or process your state machine attributes. Fix: Ensure your state machine anchor is a partial struct whose name ends in StateMachine, marked with the [LocomotionStateMachine] attribute Ensure each state is a separate partial struct marked with [LocomotionState(typeof(YourStateMachine))] Check that your project references the WAYN.Games.MGM.CharacterController.Runtime assembly Restart Unity or reimport the package - the source generator runs at compile time Verify: Check the Roslyn Analyzers section in your assembly definition to confirm the source generator DLL is referenced. Build compiles but character doesn't work in player Cause: Generic types used by the source generator may not be registered for AOT compilation. Fix: Ensure you have [assembly: RegisterGenericComponentType(typeof(LocomotionInputAsset<YourInput>))] in your assembly Check for Burst compilation errors in the build log - state methods must be Burst-compatible (no managed types) Verify there are no managed types (string, class, arrays) in state structs or context Verify: Build with Development Build enabled and check the Player log for Burst or ECS errors. Debug visualization not showing Cause: Debug components are not added or the Scene view is not visible. Fix: Select the character entity's authoring GameObject in the sub-scene Add a LocomotionDebugConfigAuthoring component Configure which visualizations to enable in the Inspector Enter Play mode and switch to the Scene view (debug gizmos do not render in Game view) Verify: Debug data is baked into a blob asset, so changes require re-entering Play mode. Next Steps Debug Visualization - Detailed guide on the debug system Physics Configuration - Tuning physical parameters Getting Started - Verify your setup is correct

manual/upgrade-guide.html.title: Upgrade Guide | MGM Character Controller
manual/upgrade-guide.html.summary: Upgrade Guide This page documents breaking changes and migration steps between versions. 0.7.0 to 0.8.0 Release date: 2026-07-28 Breaking Changes Averaged multi-character framing removed (FollowStrategy.Average) The averaged multi-character camera-framing option was removed from the public API. The FollowStrategy.Average enum member no longer exists. This member was declared but never functioned — no camera rig ever consumed it — so no runtime behaviour is lost. The replacement is primary/first-character framing (FollowStrategy.First), which is the single-target behaviour the camera rig already implements. Migration: Code — any code that referenced FollowStrategy.Average no longer compiles. Switch those references to FollowStrategy.First. Scenes / prefabs — a consumer scene or prefab that serialized FollowStrategy = Average (value 2) will deserialize an out-of-range enum value. Reset those FollowStrategy fields to First in the Inspector. FollowStrategy.None and FollowStrategy.First keep their existing values (0 and 1), so serialized data already using them is unaffected. 0.6.0 to 0.7.0 Release date: 2026-04-17 Changes BehaviorShowCase sample replaces in-package test content The previous in-package test scenes were removed and superseded by the Behavior Showcase sample: 28+ behavior subscenes plus a runtime UI Toolkit scene picker. Migration: If you relied on the old in-package test content, import Behavior Showcase from Window > Package Manager > Samples instead. Camera-up smoothing moved to CharacterFollowerSystem Camera-up smoothing logic moved into CharacterFollowerSystem, and the gravity reorient step was rescheduled for consistent timing. CameraUpSmoothing.TransitionDuration now drives ease-in/out for gravity-change camera reorientation. Migration: No API change for typical setups, but if you tuned gravity-flip camera behavior, re-verify the feel and adjust TransitionDuration. Dev-only debug visualization assets quarantined Internal debug visualization dev-assets are no longer shipped in the package. Migration: If you referenced those internal assets directly, remove the references. The LocomotionDebugConfigAuthoring workflow (Debug Visualization) is unaffected. Added Hybrid mesh rendering fallback plus fixed-step rate authoring (FixedStepRateAuthoring, see Fixed Step Rate) for GameObject↔ECS hybrid setups EditMode regression test assembly covering the character controller Fixed WebGL release crash at character spawn - hybrid transform sync no longer crashes in release builds Overlap resolution now accounts for existing ground contact; multi-plane SolveOverlaps overshoot fixed; dispose/world-teardown errors eliminated 0.5.0 to 0.6.0 Release date: 2026-04-03 Changes PostCollisionImpulse queue is deterministic The post-collision impulse storage changed from NativeParallelMultiHashMap back to a NativeQueue: impulses are now sorted before application for deterministic ordering, and the separate clear job was removed. Migration: No action needed unless you extended the impulse pipeline; if you did, update your code to the queue-based storage. ProfilerRecorderMap / LocomotionProfilerHUD removed The profiler overlay components were removed from the package. Migration: Remove any usage of ProfilerRecorderMap or LocomotionProfilerHUD. Use the Unity Profiler directly instead. Migration: In your Unity project's Packages/manifest.json, update the dependency name: // Before "com.wayngamesassets.mgm.charactercontroller": "..." // After "wayn.games.mgm.character-controller": "..." If they reference by name string, update to the new names. Before (0.3.0): public struct MyStateMachineDefinition : ILocomotionStateMachineDefinition { ... } After (0.4.0): [LocomotionStateMachine] public partial struct MyStateMachine { } Migration: Delete your old definition struct. Create a new struct with the [LocomotionStateMachine] attribute. The source generator discovers states and transitions from [LocomotionState] and [LocomotionTransition] attributes. Before (0.2.0): internal static void OnEnterState(ref MyContext ctx) { } After (0.3.0): public void OnEnterState(ref MyContext ctx) { } Migration: Change all state lifecycle methods from internal static to public instance methods. CharacterPhysicsProfile moved to ILocomotionContext CharacterPhysicsProfile is no longer part of ILocomotionProfile. It is now a property on ILocomotionContext. Before: ctx.Profile.PhysicsProfileValue After: ctx.CharacterPhysicsProfile Migration: Move physics profile access from ctx.Profile to ctx.CharacterPhysicsProfile. Remove PhysicsProfileValue from your profile struct. Base authoring classes renamed Old Name New Name BaseCharacterAuthoring BaseCharacterLocomotorAuthoring BaseCharacterBaker BaseCharacterLocomotorBaker Migration: Find-and-replace the old names in your authoring scripts. Platform velocity inheritance The path-tracking platform system was replaced with a MotionVelocity-based approach via ComputeInheritedDisplacement. Access platform data via ctx.BaseContext.PlatformHorizontalVelocity and ctx.BaseContext.PlatformVerticalVelocity. Transition evaluation timing EvaluateTransitions now runs once at the end of the execution loop (after all physics), not after each bounce iteration. Migration: If your transitions depend on mid-frame contact data, adapt them to use the final post-physics contact state instead. Recreate your state machine using the new creation menu (Assets > Create > WAYN Games > MGM Character Controller > StateMachine). manual/writing-states.html.title: Writing Custom States | MGM Character Controller
manual/writing-states.html.summary: Writing Custom States States are the building blocks of character behavior. Each state defines how the character moves, reacts to physics, and transitions to other states. This guide covers the state interface, lifecycle methods, and common patterns. The state-machine behavior guaranteed for the reference character is specified as SM-1–SM-4 in the behavior specification shipped with the package (Documentation~/spec/). The State Interface Every state is an unmanaged struct that implements ILocomotionState: [LocomotionState(typeof(MyCharacterStateMachine))] internal partial struct MyState { public void OnEnterState(ref MyContext ctx) { } public void OnIntegrateState(ref MyContext ctx) { } public void OnResolveStateCollisions(ref MyContext ctx) { } public void OnExitState(ref MyContext ctx) { } } Key rules: All lifecycle methods are instance methods with default interface implementations (DIM pattern). They are public void, not internal static. The ILocomotionState interface is added by the source generator via the partial mechanism. Transitions are handled by separate transition structs (see Transitions below) - the state struct does not define transition logic The source generator dispatches calls to the correct state struct - no virtual dispatch at runtime State methods run inside an already Burst-compiled job, so explicit [BurstCompile] on state structs and methods is not required No managed types (strings, classes, arrays) - this code runs inside Burst jobs Lifecycle Methods OnEnterState Called once when the state machine transitions into this state. Use it to: Initialize state-specific data (reset timers, counters) Set initial velocities Clear contact information (for airborne states) public void OnEnterState(ref MyContext ctx) { // Entering a grounded state: cancel all vertical momentum ctx.BaseContext.VerticalVelocity = float3.zero; ctx.BaseContext.VerticalDisplacement = float3.zero; } OnIntegrateState Called once per frame during the integration phase. This is where you compute the character's desired displacement based on input, gravity, and profile parameters. Your job here is to populate HorizontalDisplacement, VerticalDisplacement, HorizontalVelocity, and VerticalVelocity on the BaseLocomotionContext. The easiest way is to compute accelerations and call UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements: public void OnIntegrateState(ref MyContext ctx) { ref BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ref ctx.BaseContext; // Compute gravity float3 gravityAcceleration = baseContext.GravityDirection * baseContext.GravityStrength; // Compute movement acceleration from input float3 desiredVelocity = ctx.Input.MovementDirection * ctx.Profile.MaxSpeed; float accel = ctx.Profile.MaxSpeed / ctx.Profile.TimeToMaxSpeed; MathematicsHelpers.ComputeAccelerationToTargetVelocity( out float3 moveAcceleration, baseContext.HorizontalVelocity, desiredVelocity, baseContext.TimeStep, accel); // Apply both accelerations baseContext.UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements( newHorizontalAcceleration: moveAcceleration, newVerticalAcceleration: gravityAcceleration); } Important Do not add platform velocity here. The ComputeInheritedDisplacement step handles it automatically after collision resolution. Adding it manually would cause double-application. The Context Copy Pattern Because BaseLocomotionContext is a value type on the context interface, modifying it requires either: Option A: Use a ref local (when your context exposes the backing field): ref BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ref ctx.BaseContext; baseContext.HorizontalVelocity = float3.zero; // Changes are written through the ref Option B: Copy, modify, write back (when going through the interface): BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ctx.BaseContext; baseContext.HorizontalVelocity = float3.zero; ctx.BaseContext = baseContext; The sample uses ref access because the context struct exposes BaseContext as a public field in addition to the interface property. OnResolveStateCollisions Called potentially multiple times per frame (up to MaxBounce iterations). Each call represents one iteration of the collide-and-slide algorithm. In most cases, your implementation simply delegates to baseContext.Move(): public void OnResolveStateCollisions(ref MyContext ctx) { BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ctx.BaseContext; baseContext.Move(); ctx.BaseContext = baseContext; } Note You must use the copy-modify-writeback pattern here because Move() modifies the context's position, displacement, and contact data internally. For advanced use cases, you can add custom collision response logic. For example, applying an impulse to dynamic bodies the character hits: public void OnResolveStateCollisions(ref MyContext ctx) { BaseLocomotionContext baseContext = ctx.BaseContext; baseContext.Move(); // Push dynamic bodies away on contact if (baseContext.IsInContact && baseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO.BodyType == BodyType.Dynamic) { float3 pushVelocity = baseContext.HorizontalVelocity * 0.5f; baseContext.ApplyImpulse( ref baseContext, baseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO.BodyIndex, baseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO.Entity, /* impactorBodyIndex */ ..., baseContext.CharacterEntity, pushVelocity); } ctx.BaseContext = baseContext; } OnExitState Called once when the state machine transitions out of this state. Use it to clean up state-specific data: public void OnExitState(ref MyContext ctx) { // Reset jump counter when leaving the jumping state ctx.StateData.JumpData.JumpsCount = 0; } Transitions Transitions define when and how the character moves between states. Evaluation order between the transitions out of a state is controlled by ordering attributes — see Transition Ordering. Recommended: Attribute-Based Transitions Declare transitions as small structs with [LocomotionTransition]. The source generator discovers them and handles dispatch, OnExitState, and OnEnterState automatically. [LocomotionTransition(typeof(IdleState), typeof(JumpingState))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(IdleToMoving))] [EvaluateBefore(typeof(IdleToFalling))] public struct IdleToJumping : IMyTransition { public bool ShouldTransition(ref MyContext ctx) => ctx.BaseContext.IsGroundingContact && ctx.Input.JumpTrigger > 0; } Key rules: The struct name follows the {Source}To{Target} convention [LocomotionTransition(typeof(FromState), typeof(ToState))] declares which states are connected ShouldTransition returns true when the transition should fire [EvaluateBefore] / [EvaluateAfter] control priority - the first matching transition wins The source generator calls OnExitState on the source and OnEnterState on the target automatically See the sample's Runtime/States/Transitions/ folder for a complete example with 17 transitions, split across one file per source state (FromIdling.cs, FromMoving.cs, ...) plus grouped target files (ToJumping.cs, ToFalling.cs, ToSliding.cs). The attribute-based pattern is the only supported approach. The source generator discovers all [LocomotionTransition] structs, handles exit/enter calls, and makes transition priority explicit via [EvaluateBefore]/[EvaluateAfter] attributes. Consuming Trigger Input Trigger inputs like jump presses must be consumed after use. Otherwise, the trigger fires every frame: static void ConsumeJumpTrigger(ref MyContext ctx) { MyInput value = ctx.Input; value.JumpTrigger = 0; ctx.Input = value; } Call this in OnIntegrateState after using the trigger value. The copy-modify-writeback pattern is required because Input is a value type on the context. Reusing Logic Across States States share logic by composing behavior structs - small stateless structs with configuration fields and an Integrate method that returns an acceleration. The sample defines three in Runtime/States/Behaviors/: GravityBehavior (shared by Falling and Sliding), HorizontalLocomotionBehavior (shared by Moving and Jumping), and JumpBehavior (the full jump-arc lifecycle). Each state constructs the behaviors it needs from its profile data, calls Integrate, and commits the result. From the sample's Jumping state: public void OnIntegrateState(ref SimpleCharacterContext ctx) { ref var profile = ref ctx.Profile.Value; ref var moving = ref profile.Moving; // Horizontal air control — ground feel scaled by AirControlFactor (0 = ballistic, 1 = full). float3 horizontalAcceleration = new HorizontalLocomotionBehavior { Speed = math.select(moving.WalkSpeed, moving.RunSpeed, ctx.Input.IsSprinting), TimeToTargetSpeed = moving.TimeToTargetSpeed, TimeToStop = moving.TimeToStop, RotateCharacterToMovement = true, }.Integrate(ref ctx) * profile.AirControlFactor; // Vertical lifecycle — trigger, variable-height ascent, apex hover, descent. float3 verticalAcceleration = new JumpBehavior().Integrate(ref ctx); ctx.BaseContext.UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements(horizontalAcceleration, verticalAcceleration); } The behavior owns the integration math; the state owns the composition and the commit via UpdateVelocitiesAndComputeDisplacements. This keeps the physics logic in one place while each state stays a thin, readable composition. Do not share state data this way - each state manages its own initialization and cleanup via OnEnterState / OnExitState. Common State Patterns Grounded State (Idle / Moving) OnEnterState: Zero out vertical velocity OnIntegrateState: Compute horizontal acceleration only Transitions: Check for jump input, loss of ground contact, slope above max Airborne State (Falling / Jumping) OnEnterState: Clear contact (LocomotionContact.None), optionally inherit platform velocity OnIntegrateState: Apply gravity + optional air control Transitions: Check for ground contact, wall contact Sliding State OnIntegrateState: Apply gravity (character slides down slope) Transitions: Check for loss of contact (to falling), ground contact below max slope (to moving/idle) Custom State Ideas Wall Running: Enter when jumping into a wall at speed; apply gravity slowly; allow wall jump Dashing: Enter on trigger; apply burst horizontal velocity; exit after timer Swimming: Enter when submerged; replace gravity with buoyancy; allow 3D movement Climbing: Enter at ladder; disable gravity; move along ladder axis Debugging States If your state isn't behaving as expected: Check transition priority order - an earlier transition might be firing first Log baseContext.LocomotionContact.ValueRO.ContactType to verify contact detection Verify that OnExitState and OnEnterState are called during transitions Ensure trigger inputs are accumulated in ApplyInputsToCharacter and consumed in OnIntegrateState Use the debug visualization to see contact points, movement paths, and impulses Next Steps The Execution Loop - When exactly each method is called Physics Configuration - Tuning capsule and collision parameters Recipe: Add a New State - Step-by-step guide to adding a state Best Practices - Recommended patterns for state logic
